articles.title: Proxmox 9.3 adds production snapshots for SAN-backed VMs
articles.context: 3 adds production support for snapshots on shared LVM storage over iSCSI and Fibre Channel SANs
articles.full_text:
Proxmox Virtual Environment 9.3 adds production support for snapshots on shared LVM storage over iSCSI and Fibre Channel SANs. The open-source virtualization platform also gives each guest an identity that survives migration, backup and restore.

If your VMs sit on a SAN, you can now snapshot them before a risky change in a setup the vendor supports for production. The snapshots work as volume chains on thick-provisioned LVM, the layer that carves SAN disks into guest storage. Admins turn it on in the advanced storage settings with the “Allow Snapshots as Volume-Chain” option.

The guest identity matters for backups. It stays the same even when a guest gets a new VMID or is restored to another cluster, so backup software and outside management tools can recognize the same machine across its life.

SAN setup moves into the web interface

Multipath means several network routes to the same storage LUN, and admins used to configure it node by node. A guided workflow now sets it up across cluster nodes for iSCSI, Fibre Channel and NVMe over Fabrics. A new Datacenter > SAN view shows LUN path state across all nodes in real time.

New logs and network isolation

The web interface gains a color-coded, filterable System Log, an API Access Log, and an APT History of past package transactions and changelogs. Simple SDN zones can use a dedicated VRF, a separate routing table, with custom static routes. WireGuard fabrics report interface and peer status.

Ceph key rotation is still a preview

Ceph Umbrella 21.2 ships as a technology preview, with a hardened default cipher for CephX authentication and online key rotation for daemons. Preview status means you test it before trusting it. Ceph Tentacle 20.2 is the stable version.

Underneath, 9.3 runs on Debian 13.8 with Linux kernel 7.0 as the default and kernel 7.3 as an opt-in. Upgrades from older versions run through APT, and a full ISO installs on bare metal.

articles.title: Introducing Wiz ADR: Strengthening Cloud and AI Detection and Response with Application Context
articles.context: AI-assisted attacks have dramatically compressed the time from vulnerability disclosure to active exploitation–meaning attackers routinely reach execution faster than...
articles.full_text:
The security tools SecOps teams rely on have gotten exceptionally good at detecting infrastructure-level events: subprocess spawns, outbound network connections, and system calls. However, what has historically been missing is visibility into the application layer sitting directly above those events: which specific function executed the call, how code execution reached that point, and whether the observed runtime behavior represents expected application logic or an active exploit in progress.

This visibility gap is becoming increasingly critical to address. AI-assisted attacks have dramatically compressed the time from vulnerability disclosure to active exploitation–meaning attackers routinely reach execution faster than engineering teams can patch. At the same time, modern threats like compromised dependencies and prompt-injected AI agents execute entirely inside legitimate application processes without a CVE at all. When every minute counts, deep application context lets SecOps teams immediately separate real attacks from benign app behavior, pinpoint how execution happened, and respond without delay.

Today, we are excited to announce Wiz ADR (Application Detection and Response). Built directly into the Wiz Runtime Sensor, Wiz ADR brings application-layer visibility into threat detection–pairing application call stacks with OS and process telemetry, with no extra agents or code changes required. Rather than only alerting on suspicious events at the system layer, Wiz ADR reveals the exact functions that triggered them–helping SecOps cut false positives by seeing the application’s true intent, and simplifying the handoff to engineering by pinpointing the exact line of code to fix.

Wiz ADR: Turning Runtime Alerts into Clear Intent and Fast Fixes

Whenever a runtime detection fires across your workloads, the Wiz Runtime Sensor doesn’t stop at the OS process–it reaches into the application layer to capture what your code was doing at the exact moment the event occurred.

Wiz ADR reconstructs the application call stack both inside the process that triggered the alert and across parent-to-child spawns–so even when a web service launches a child shell command, analysts see the exact application function that kicked it off. Along the way, it flags meaningful execution patterns with application context tags (such as Request Handler, Dynamic Code Execution, or Unsafe Deserialization), translating raw function calls into plain-English security signals so SecOps can spot the root cause immediately, even without knowing the underlying codebase. When those context tags appear on a runtime event, the Sensor also uses them directly to trigger high-fidelity application detections and elevate the severity of existing alerts.

Paired with the broader Wiz Platform, that application context turns ambiguous alerts into confirmed verdicts and code-level fixes across two everyday scenarios.

Confirming a Real Exploit with Wiz Blue Agent

Consider a containerized Python FastAPI service that unexpectedly spawns /usr/bin/id as root. On its own, /user/bin/id is too common across Linux workloads for standard OS-level rules to alert on without flooding the SOC–meaning early post-exploitation reconnaissance routinely slips by unnoticed.

With Wiz ADR, the Sensor sees where execution started. It reconstructs the call stack across the process spawn–tracing /user/bin/id back to the import_spellbook HTTP endpoint and into PyYAML’s UnsafeConstructor, attaches context tags like Request Handler, Python Request Handler Descendant, and Unsafe Deserialization, and fires a High-severity alert immediately.

Bringing that stack-trace analysis together with process ancestry and cloud risk gives the Wiz Blue Agent the context to classify the alert as Malicious with high confidence, connecting the application context to root execution inside a privileged production container and pointing teams directly to the import_spellbook endpoint. From there, Wiz Workflows can notify the right teams with full context and trigger response actions to contain the threat immediately.

Eliminating False Positives and Tracing Threats Straight to Code

Now consider the flip side: internal services whose legitimate code triggers scary OS alerts. When repohygiene–a containerized Go service on CI runners–runs find /data -name .git-credentials -type f during post-build audits, OS-level rules flag it as potential credential harvesting.

Pairing Wiz ADR with Wiz Code unlocks Threat to Code correlation, tracing the Go call stack (Scanner.findGitCredentials) straight back to the exact repository, file (scanner.go, line 55) and code owner in GitHub, surfacing the developer’s own code and comments right inside the alert inside of handing engineering a bare container ID and PID.

And with Blue Agent, no human has to triage it manually. Wiz Blue Agent synthesizes the stack trace, clean process ancestry (systemd -> containerd -> runc -> repohygine -> find), and sensor forensics to confirm the activity matches intended application logic, automatically classifying the alert as Not Malicious and deprioritizing it before it burns SecOps hours.

Start Defending Your Environment with Application Context

Wiz ADR is available now through the Wiz Runtime Sensor–giving SecOps and Engineering teams deep application context on runtime detections with no code changes or extra agents required.

Existing Wiz customers can learn more about Wiz ADR in our documentation, and if you are not a customer and want to see it in action please request a demo.

articles.title: Introducing Socket Calm: A Syntax Highlighting Theme for VS Code, Vim, and Neovim
articles.context: Socket Calm is also available as a standalone color scheme for Vim and Neovim, with support for true-color and 256-color terminals
articles.full_text:
We're bringing a little bit of Socket's design system to your code editor. Today we're releasing Socket Calm, a free, open source syntax highlighting theme for VS Code, Vim, and Neovim.

The theme borrows from a principle behind Socket's own interface design: use color with intention and reserve stronger visual cues for things that need your attention. The name Calm also captures what we want our products to bring to developers: peace of mind in an increasingly hostile software supply chain.

Socket Calm takes a minimalist approach to syntax highlighting with a six-color palette. Operators, punctuation, and variables retain the default foreground color, while keywords, function calls, strings, keys, and literals are distinguished by color. Additional accents are reserved for diagnostics, Git decorations, diffs, and terminal output.

The theme comes in two variants, featuring the warm plum and sand backgrounds from Socket's design system, with semantic highlighting enabled by default.

Socket Calm Dark

Socket Calm Light

Try Socket Calm

#

VS Code users can install Socket Calm directly from the Visual Studio Marketplace and select either the light or dark variant.

Socket Calm is also available as a standalone color scheme for Vim and Neovim, with support for true-color and 256-color terminals.

The theme is released under the MIT license. You can find the source code, installation instructions, and configuration options on GitHub.

articles.title: Introducing Search for Agents
articles.context: Still, setting up an AI Search instance for your website requires manually creating and configuring it initially, and then doing all the integration work to get the search...
articles.full_text:
AI Search, our service that indexes your content and lets you add search to any application or agent without having to build an entire retrieval infrastructure, has supported adding your website as a data source for a while now, automatically crawling, converting and indexing its pages.

Still, setting up an AI Search instance for your website requires manually creating and configuring it initially, and then doing all the integration work to get the search endpoints available from your domain and to make sure that agents know where to find the index and know how to use it.

Today we're introducing Search for Agents, which puts that setup behind a toggle in your Cloudflare dashboard. Turn it on for your zone, and our service will create your AI Search instance, start indexing your content, and make search discoverable and available from your own domain.

How it works

The idea follows naturally from Markdown for Agents, where Cloudflare's network converts any HTML page to Markdown in real time for enabled zones using content negotiation headers. Similarly, Search for Agents leverages the power of AI Search by automatically creating an index for your zone and exposing APIs that any AI agent can discover and use to search your website, under your domain, all done at the network level.

You can enable Search for Agents using the API, or by going to the dashboard in your zone page, under Quick Actions:

Search for Agents is available to all customers, including Free (with limits). Once it’s enabled, Cloudflare will automatically create an AI Search instance, start crawling and indexing the content in your zone. Refer to our developer documentation to understand how the crawling process works.

You can access your instance directly from this page, or by going to directly to your account’s AI > AI Search instances view:

The AI Search instance for your zone is created with default settings, but you can enable reranking or change configuration options like cache settings at any time. Refer to our documentation for the full list of options.

Once AI Search indexes your content, you or any agent on the Internet can start using Search for Agents, subject to your domain settings (e.g. your bot management settings, AI Crawl Control and web application firewall (WAF) configurations).

Discoverability

Search isn't much use if the agents don’t know it's there. To facilitate discoverability, Search for Agents automatically advertises the search endpoint on every page of your site.

For example, for HTML responses, we add metadata to the page's <head>:

<meta name="agent:instructions" content="Use this search API to find relevant content across this site with keywords or natural-language queries, instead of crawling individual pages. Results are returned in Markdown."> <meta name="agent:endpoint" content="https://developers.cloudflare.com/.well-known/search?q={query}"> <meta name="agent:method" content="GET"> <meta name="agent:documentation" content="https://developers.cloudflare.com/ai-search/how-to/search-for-agents/">

If you also have Markdown for Agents enabled, an agent requesting a page with Accept: text/markdown receives the same information in YAML front matter:

--- agent: instructions: "Use this search API to find relevant content across this site with keywords or natural-language queries, instead of crawling individual pages. Results are returned in Markdown." endpoint: "https://developers.cloudflare.com/.well-known/search?q={query}" method: "GET" documentation: "https://developers.cloudflare.com/ai-search/how-to/search-for-agents/" ---

The agent will easily pick up these instructions and know what to do next to search your site.

Searching content

Once the agent knows that your site has a search endpoint, it can start using it:

$ curl "https://developers.cloudflare.com/.well-known/search?q=cloudflare+artifacts" # Search results for: "cloudflare artifacts" ## docs/artifacts/api/workers-binding/index.md (score: 1.000) # Workers binding · Artifacts · Cloudflare Artifacts docs Call Artifacts from a Worker binding. --- ## docs/artifacts/index.md (score: 0.951) # Artifacts · Cloudflare Artifacts docs Store, version, and share filesystem artifacts across Workers, APIs, and Git-compatible tools. ...

Depending on your AI Search configuration, the agent can also use natural language and ask questions to the search endpoint:

$ curl --get "https://developers.cloudflare.com/.well-known/search" --data-urlencode "q=What is the maximum push size for Cloudflare Artifacts?" # Search results for: "What is the maximum push size for Cloudflare Artifacts?" ## docs/artifacts/platform/limits/index.limits-cloudflare-artifacts-docs.md (score: 1.000) # Limits · Cloudflare Artifacts docs Section: Limits · Cloudflare Artifacts docs title: Limits description: Review Artifacts platform limits. pcx_content_type: reference products: - artifacts Limits that apply to creating, importing, cloning, and pushing Artifacts are detailed below. These limits cover naming rules, storage, request rates for control-plane and Git operations, and the size of each push. FeatureLimitControl-plane request rate2,000 requests per 10 seconds per Artifacts namespaceGit request rate, per artifact2,000 requests per 10 seconds per artifactMaximum storage per repository1 GB for repos created on or after 2026-09-29. Repos created earlier have a 10 GB limit. See size limit change.Maximum storage per account1 TB (can be raised on request)Maximum number of repositoriesUnlimitedMaximum number of namespacesUnlimitedNamespace name length2–63 charactersNamespace and repo namesStart with a letter or digit. Remaining characters may include letters, digits, ., _, and -.Maximum push size64 MiB per push. Includes all data sent in the push. Split larger work into several smaller pushes.Maximum objects per push50,000 objects, such as file versions, folders, and commits.Maximum file size32 MiB per file. Already-compressed files, like images, video, or zip archives, may be rejected slightly below 32 MiB.Maximum ref updates per push1 MiB of branch and tag updates per push.Maximum entries per folder100,000 files and subfolders in a single folder. ...

Note that this search endpoint returns retrieved content, in Markdown, not a generated answer. The agent already has an AI model and a conversation with the user; all it needs is the relevant information from your site, not another AI model's attempt to answer on its behalf.

Supporting a new HTTP method: QUERY

The new HTTP QUERY method is an IETF Proposed Standard, incidentally coauthored by our own James Snell, published in June 2026 as RFC 10008. A QUERY allows a client to send search criteria in a request body safely and idempotently without modifying server state. This makes it a good fit for AI search.

The adoption of QUERY is underway with major browser vendors discussing the RFC and multiple frameworks and clients either adopting (curl and undici, for example), or discussing adoption.

Search for Agents supports QUERY natively either using a plain text or JSON request body:

# Plain text curl -X QUERY 'https://developers.cloudflare.com/.well-known/search' \ --data 'What is the maximum payload size per ingestion request in Basin Pipelines?' # JSON curl -X QUERY 'https://developers.cloudflare.com/.well-known/search' \ --header 'Content-Type: application/json' \ --data '{"q":"How many bulk import requests per minute does Email Service allow?"}'

See it in action

Let’s see it in action during an agentic session. Search for Agents is enabled for our Developer Documentation. When we open an OpenCode session and ask “What is the maximum push size for Cloudflare Artifacts?”, in the logs we can see the agent discovering the search endpoint on the homepage and then fetching /.well-known/search with the question for the search results.

The answer comes back a few seconds later and it’s correct.

Once the agent discovers the search API, it will likely reuse it multiple times within the same session whenever it needs to search for content in the same site.

We enabled Search for Agents for our developer documentation ahead of this announcement and we’ve found that agents do a good job of discovering the search API and using it during their tasks.

It’s still an AI Search instance

Because Search for Agents is powered by an AI Search instance in your account, you get all the standard configuration options and features as well. For example, you can enable public REST API or MCP endpoints, or use it from Workers, or even embed AI Search on your website for human visitors.

Start using Search for Agents

Starting today, Search for Agents is available to all customers. The usage follows the AI Search pricing; that includes ingesting content, storing the index's content, and serving queries, subject to the account's included usage and limits for both the Workers Free and Paid plans.

We also recommend you check our Agent Readiness page (see announcement) and understand how you can make your sites optimized for agents, from guiding agents on how to authenticate, to controlling what content agents can see, the format they receive it in, and how they pay for it.

Check out the Search for Agents developer docs for more information. Follow us on X or come and talk to us in the Cloudflare Developer Discord. We'd like to hear from site owners making their content searchable to agents.

articles.title: Introducing context-aware rules for AWS Network Firewall
articles.context: A rule that names a subnet or VPC applies to each new resource that you launch in it
articles.full_text:
AWS Network Firewall now supports context-aware rules, which match traffic by the AWS resources that send and receive it instead of by IP address. A rule can name a virtual private cloud (VPC), a subnet, a security group, or a transit gateway attachment. Rules that match on IP addresses have to keep up with every workload that scales out, is replaced, or moves. Short-lived workloads are the hardest to keep up with. A VPC-attached AWS Lambda function can scale out and start sending traffic before an updated IP list reaches the firewall. With context-aware rules, you can filter a function’s traffic by the security group attached to it.

With context-aware rules, you can:

Write rules that follow your workloads – A rule that names a security group applies to each new resource whose network interface has that security group attached. A rule that names a subnet or VPC applies to each new resource that you launch in it. A rule that names a transit gateway attachment applies to traffic that enters through that attachment.

Apply one policy across accounts – One context store tracks the resources in the accounts that attach to a shared transit gateway. A rule can name context from any of those accounts.

See which resources are behind each connection – Your firewall logs record the resources on each side of a flow, along with their IP addresses.

In this post, we explain how context-aware rules work, set them up across accounts, and show what the logs record.

How context-aware rules work

Context-aware rules require transit gateway-attached firewalls, and they combine a control path and a data path (Figure 1). On the control path, a context store tells the firewall which AWS resources exist. On the data path, the transit gateway adds the context of the sender to each packet. The firewall brings the two together and matches that context against your rules.

Figure 1: How context-aware rules work across accounts

A context store tracks your resources. A context store is a catalog of the AWS resources that can send and receive traffic through a transit gateway. You create it in AWS Network Manager and associate it with the transit gateway that your firewall uses. When you share the transit gateway with workload accounts through AWS Resource Access Manager (AWS RAM), those accounts create transit gateway VPC attachments to it. The context of those attachments, and of the resources behind them, then appears in the same context store. The context store is designed to keep the firewall in sync as you add and remove resources.

The transit gateway tags each packet. When traffic crosses the transit gateway, the transit gateway tags each packet with the context of the resource that sent it. That context is the sender’s VPC, subnet, transit gateway attachment, and the security groups attached to the sender. The firewall gets only the security group IDs, not their rules, so a rule that names any one of those groups matches.

The firewall matches context IDs in your rules. It reads the context on each packet and matches it against your rules. You group context IDs into a context set, a named rule variable that lists resources from the context store associated with the firewall. Then you use the set in the source or destination of a rule, in a Classic or Next Generation firewall policy.

Source context works with every protocol, because each packet carries the context of its sender. Destination context requires TCP-based rules, because the firewall learns the receiving resource from return traffic. For more details, see How context-aware rules work and Matching on destination context. AWS Transit Gateway also shares context with third-party firewalls through Gateway Load Balancer. For that setup, see Introducing resource context for firewall policies with AWS Transit Gateway.

Getting started

In this example, a central networking account owns the transit gateway and the firewall, and shares the transit gateway with workload accounts through AWS RAM. You complete steps 1 and 2 once, in the account that owns the transit gateway.

1. Create a context store. In the AWS Network Manager console, select or create a global network and register your transit gateway with it. Then create a context store and associate it with the transit gateway (). Network Firewall discovers the context store on its own, so there’s nothing to configure on the firewall.

Figure 2: A context store associated with a transit gateway

2. Give Network Firewall access to the context store. In the account that owns the context store, create the AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) role NetworkFirewallContextStoreReadOnly. Use the trust policy and permissions in Onboarding your transit gateway to a context store. You create the role once for each account that owns a context store.

3. Create a context set. In the Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (Amazon VPC) console, under Network Firewall, create a rule group. On the Rule group variables page, choose Create context set, select your context store, and select the resources for the set. One set can mix context IDs of different resource types, from the accounts in the context store.

Figure 3: Creating a context set from the resources that the context store tracks

4. Check the sync state. Before you write rules, open the firewall’s details page and check the Context store sync state section. It shows the context store that the firewall discovered and its sync state.

Figure 4: The context store sync state on the firewall’s details page

5. Use the context set in your rules. The sample rule from Writing context-aware rules blocks SSH from PROD_RESOURCES to destinations outside your home networks. In a Next Generation firewall rule group, on the Configure rules page, use the Visual rule builder. Choose Drop and TCP. For Sources, choose Match specific criteria, select Context sets, and choose PROD_RESOURCES. For Destinations, choose Match specific criteria, select Destination IP, and enter $EXTERNAL_NET. Set the destination port to 22. Then add the rule group to your firewall policy.

Figure 5: Choosing a context set as a rule’s source in the Next Generation rule builder

The same rule in Suricata-compatible syntax follows. drop:flow is the action and its scope, tcp:all the protocol and connection state, and the rest is the source, destination, and port. In raw rules, you reference a context set with $ and its name; in the console, you pick it from a list.

drop:flow tcp:all $PROD_RESOURCES any -> $EXTERNAL_NET 22 (msg:"Block SSH from production to external"; sid:2001;)

Because the rule names resources and not addresses, it covers each new resource that you launch in those VPCs or attach that security group to.

For Classic policies, the same rule looks like this:

drop tcp $PROD_RESOURCES any -> $EXTERNAL_NET 22 (msg:"Block SSH from production to external"; sid:2001; rev:1;)

What the logs record

After you associate the transit gateway with a context store, Network Firewall adds a context object to its alert log and flow log records. The following records, shortened, show one outbound TLS connection from an application instance to example.com, through a central egress VPC with a network address translation (NAT) gateway. A rule that references the application’s security group blocks the connection and writes this alert log record. The matched list names the security group that the rule matched.

{ "event": { "event_type": "alert", "flow_id": 314246768212473, "src_ip": "10.1.1.25", "dest_ip": "203.0.113.10", "dest_port": 443, "app_proto": "tls", "tls": { "sni": "example.com" }, "context": { "matched": [ "sg-0a1b2c3d4e5f60031" ] }, "alert": { "action": "blocked", "signature_id": 2002, "signature": "Application A: domain not on its allow list" } } }

The flow log record for the same flow_id lists the full context on each side. The src list holds the sender’s context IDs. Flow logs record this context for every flow, even when no rule matches it.

{ "event": { "event_type": "netflow", "flow_id": 314246768212473, "src_ip": "10.1.1.25", "dest_ip": "203.0.113.10", "dest_port": 443, "app_proto": "tls", "context": { "src": [ "vpc-0a1b2c3d4e5f60001", "subnet-0a1b2c3d4e5f60011", "tgw-attach-0a1b2c3d4e5f60021", "sg-0a1b2c3d4e5f60031" ], "dst": [ "vpc-0a1b2c3d4e5f60003", "subnet-0a1b2c3d4e5f60013", "tgw-attach-0a1b2c3d4e5f60023" ] } } }

The dst list shows how destination context works for traffic to the internet. The firewall learns the destination from the response, and the response reaches the firewall from the NAT gateway. So the destination context is the egress VPC, the NAT gateway’s subnet, and the egress VPC’s transit gateway attachment, not the internet host. You can query these fields by context ID in Amazon CloudWatch Logs Insights. For example, you can see what an application already connects to before you write its rules. For the fields, see Context in your network firewall logs.

Availability and pricing

Context-aware rules are available at no additional charge. Standard AWS Network Firewall and AWS Transit Gateway charges apply to the resources that you use. For details, see AWS Network Firewall pricing and AWS Transit Gateway pricing. They work in the AWS Regions where both Network Firewall and Transit Gateway context sharing are available.

Conclusion

In this post, we showed how you can use context-aware rules in Network Firewall to match traffic on the context of the resources that send and receive traffic. A context store tracks those resources across the accounts that share your transit gateway, and the transit gateway tags each packet with its sender’s context. Your rules and logs then use that context, so your rules can keep up as workloads change. To learn more, see Context-aware rules in AWS Network Firewall.

If you have questions about this post, contact AWS Support or start a new thread on AWS re:Post.

articles.title: Introducing AWS Network Firewall Next Generation policy
articles.context: They want to allow only the traffic each application needs, and they want each allowed connection checked for known threats
articles.full_text:
When it comes to inspecting network traffic, many security teams want two things from a firewall. They want to allow only the traffic each application needs, and they want each allowed connection checked for known threats. Today, you can do both with AWS Network Firewall, a stateful, managed network firewall and intrusion detection and prevention service. In a Classic policy, your access rules and your threat rules run together in one stateful engine and share one rule capacity.

With Next Generation policies, access control and threat protection each get their own engine in the same firewall. A firewall engine allows the traffic you approve and drops the rest. An intrusion prevention system (IPS) engine checks the allowed traffic with AWS managed rule groups or with rules that you write. Each engine has its own rule capacity, so adding access rules doesn’t take capacity away from threat protection.

In this post, we walk through what Next Generation policies are, how they evaluate traffic, and the new concepts they introduce. We use sample records to cover what each engine logs and how to validate a policy with the new monitor mode. To put it all together, we walk through creating an example Next Generation policy.

How a Next Generation policy works

A Next Generation policy inspects traffic with two engines, in sequence. Traffic that the firewall engine allows moves to the IPS engine, and traffic that the firewall engine blocks goes no further. The firewall engine is drop by default, and the IPS engine is pass by default.

If you already write Suricata rules, the two engines will feel familiar. The firewall engine is built on Suricata 8 firewall mode, which follows each connection as it progresses and evaluates rules at each step. The IPS engine uses the Suricata compatible intrusion detection system (IDS) and IPS rules that you already know from the stateful engine in a Classic policy, with one difference: it evaluates rules in action order and doesn’t support Classic options such as strict order.

A Classic policy uses a stateless engine and then a stateful engine that evaluates access rules and threat rules together. In a Next Generation policy, both engines are stateful, so each rule is evaluated with full connection context, which helps keep traffic handling consistent and predictable. The firewall engine works up to the application layer. It follows each connection for its entire flow, from the first packet through the TCP handshake and application layer exchanges such as the TLS client hello, and evaluates your access rules along the way (Figure 1).

Figure 1: Classic and Next Generation policy engines and their rule capacity.

This separation changes how you design a policy. Because each engine has one job, you can plan access control and threat protection on their own, and different teams can work independently. For example, a networking team can manage access rules while a security team handles threat detection, and neither has to rewrite the other’s rules.

The firewall engine controls access

You configure access control by specifying an action for a protocol, along with a source and destination. Rules run in the order that you set. Traffic that no rule allows gets the policy’s firewall default action, which is drop unless you change it. In a Next Generation policy, the drop default action applies from the first packet, so for TCP traffic the firewall can drop the initial SYN. Unlike the drop established default action in a Classic policy, it doesn’t wait for a connection to be established.

A few terms explain how the firewall engine evaluates traffic. Connection states are the protocol states that a connection progresses through, such as the TCP handshake and the TLS client hello. A hook is the point at a connection state where your rules attach, so a rule’s hook sets when the firewall engine evaluates it. Each rule also has an action, such as accept, drop, or reject. Its action scope sets how much of the traffic the action applies to, from one packet or one transaction up to the whole connection, called the flow. For more details, see Firewall engine hooks.

When you build a rule in the console, you choose a protocol and then two settings: Connection state, which sets the rule’s hook, and Action scope. For example, to allow a domain over TLS, you match its server name at the Client Hello connection state with the This flow action scope.

Because the firewall engine is drop by default, a connection advances to the next connection state only while your rules keep accepting it. For example, a connection can pass the TCP handshake and still be dropped at the TLS client hello. That happens when its server name isn’t on your approved list (Figure 2).

Figure 2: A connection is accepted at the TCP handshake hook and dropped at the TLS client hello hook.

In Figure 2, the rule for www.amazon.com accepts the flow when it matches the server name at the TLS client hello hook. No rule accepts example.com at that hook, so the firewall default action drops it.

You don’t have to write every rule in raw Suricata syntax. You can build rules in the console rule builder, or, as in the example later in this post, enter your domains in a domain list rule group, and Network Firewall builds the rules for you.

Action scope also sets where an accepted connection goes next. An accept with the hook scope allows the connection to advance to the next connection state, where the rules at that hook evaluate it. An accept with the flow scope lets the connection skip the remaining hooks and move to the IPS engine (Figure 3). A firewall rule can also bypass the IPS engine for specific traffic when you choose. For the valid combinations of action and scope at each type of hook, see Firewall engine actions and scopes.

Figure 3: An accept with the hook scope compared with an accept with the flow scope.

The IPS engine looks for threats

Traffic that the firewall engine allows then reaches the IPS engine, which inspects it with Suricata compatible rules. The IPS engine is designed to look for specific threats, so it blocks only traffic that matches a threat rule. IPS rules evaluate in action order. Pass rules go first, then drop, reject, and alert rules, regardless of the order in which you define them. For the full path through both engines, see How Network Firewall filters traffic with a Next Generation policy.

We recommend that you start with the AWS managed rule groups. Because the IPS engine is built on the industry standard Suricata engine, you can also run Suricata compatible rule sets from specialized security providers, alongside rules that you write yourself.

Referenced rule groups and embedded rules

Each engine gets its rules from its own section of the policy. You can add rules in two ways and mix both in one section.

Referenced rule groups are separate resources, and they’re the only kind of rule group that Classic policies support. You create a rule group once and add it to as many policies as you need. You can also share it with other accounts through AWS Resource Access Manager (AWS RAM). For details, see Sharing AWS Network Firewall resources. When you update the rule group, each policy that references it picks up the change. You set a referenced rule group’s capacity when you create it, and you can’t change it afterward, so leave room for it to grow.

Embedded rules are new with Next Generation policies. You write them directly inside one policy, and they belong to that policy only, so you can’t share them with another policy. Use them to add rules quickly that are specific to that policy. They use that engine’s rule capacity, and you don’t set a capacity up front. Embedded rules in both engine sections share a combined limit. For all limits, see AWS Network Firewall quotas.

Read what each engine logs

Whichever way you add rules, both engines write to the same alert and flow logs, which you configure in the logging configuration. Each alert record carries new fields that show which engine wrote it and, for the firewall engine, the hook where the decision happened.

The following record came from a test, in enforce mode, of the example policy that you build later in this post. A host tried to reach example.com, which isn’t on the allow list.

{ "firewall_name": "example-fw", "availability_zone": "us-east-1a", "event_timestamp": "1794341434", "event": { "event_type": "alert", "app_proto": "tls", "src_ip": "10.0.1.25", "src_port": 42698, "dest_ip": "203.0.113.10", "dest_port": 443, "proto": "TCP", "tls": { "sni": "example.com" }, "alert": { "engine": "fw", "action": "blocked", "signature_id": 2201001, "signature": "SURICATA FW default app policy", "severity": 3 }, "firewall": { "hook": "tls:client_hello", "policy": "drop:flow,alert" }, "verdict": { "action": "drop" }, "aws_metadata": { "resource_arn": "arn:aws:network-firewall:us-east-1:111122223333:firewall-policy-v2/example-policy" }, "timestamp": "2026-11-10T20:10:34.141643+0000" } }

The following table explains the key fields in this record.

Field

Value

What it tells you

alert.engine

The firewall engine wrote this record.

firewall.hook

tls:client_hello

The decision happened at the TLS client hello, where the client sends the server name example.com.

alert.signature

No rule matched, so the firewall default action applied. The default action logs its drops on its own, so you don’t need an alert rule to see what it blocks.

firewall.policy

The action and scope that applied. The default action dropped the whole flow and wrote an alert.

The policy itself is the source, because the record doesn’t come from one of your rule groups.

When a connection that the firewall engine allowed matches a threat rule, the IPS engine writes its own record. In this test, the firewall engine allowed TLS to one test server by IP address. The IPS section also held the following embedded rule, which drops TLS connections with a JA4 fingerprint that your threat intelligence flags. The fingerprint in this rule is a sample value:

drop tls $HOME_NET any -> $EXTERNAL_NET any (msg:"Example: flagged TLS client fingerprint (JA4)"; flow:to_server,established; ja4.hash; content:"t13d1516h2_aaaaaaaaaaaa_bbbbbbbbbbbb"; classtype:trojan-activity; sid:900002; rev:1;)

This is a sample rule to show the IPS engine at work. In your own policies, we recommend that you start with the AWS managed threat signature rule groups and add custom rules where you need them.

A test client with that fingerprint connected to that server without a server name, and the IPS engine wrote the following record.

{ "firewall_name": "example-fw", "availability_zone": "us-east-1a", "event_timestamp": "1794377726", "event": { "event_type": "alert", "app_proto": "tls", "src_ip": "10.0.1.25", "src_port": 38342, "dest_ip": "198.51.100.7", "dest_port": 443, "proto": "TCP", "tls": { "version": "TLS 1.3", "ja4": "t13d1516h2_aaaaaaaaaaaa_bbbbbbbbbbbb" }, "alert": { "engine": "td", "action": "blocked", "signature_id": 900002, "signature": "Example: flagged TLS client fingerprint (JA4)"", "category": "A Network Trojan was detected", "severity": 1 }, "verdict": { "action": "drop" }, "aws_metadata": { "resource_arn": "arn:aws:network-firewall:us-east-1:111122223333:firewall-policy-v2/example-policy" }, "timestamp": "2026-11-11T06:15:26.671435+0000" } }

The rule is embedded in the policy, so the record shows the policy ARN. A match from an AWS managed rule group or one of your referenced rule groups carries that rule group’s ARN instead.

To separate access control events from threat events in your queries, filter on the engine field. To find which rule group produced an event, use resource_arn. Embedded rules and the default action show the policy ARN.

Validate in monitor mode, then enforce

Each Next Generation policy has a policy mode, enforce or monitor. In enforce mode, the engines apply their actions. In monitor mode, both engines evaluate your traffic and log what they would do. Your rules and the default action don’t drop or reject traffic.

Monitor mode also turns on alert logging for your rules and the default action, so each firewall rule that would block traffic logs its matches. That makes monitor mode a lower-risk way to stage a rollout of a new policy or a change to an existing one. Monitor logs are close to enforce mode but can differ. When a firewall rule would block a connection, monitor mode lets the connection through but sends it past the IPS engine, just as a blocked connection never reaches the IPS engine in enforce mode. So the monitor logs don’t show IPS alerts for that connection. For the full list of differences, see Policy mode: enforce and monitor.

To validate a policy in monitor mode:

Set Policy mode to Monitor, and confirm that alert logging is on for the firewall. Amazon Route 53 Resolved IP Validation still applies its configured action in monitor mode, so if your policy uses it, set its action to Alert.

Send representative traffic for long enough to cover your normal patterns.

In your alert logs, filter on engine = fw. Check the FirewallDefaultActionApplied metric in Amazon CloudWatch. Traffic that you meant to allow shouldn’t be reaching the default action.

When the results look right, switch Policy mode to Enforce during a maintenance window. Changing the policy mode or the firewall default action restarts stateful inspection on the firewall, which interrupts established connections.

Example policy with a domain allow list and threat protection

The following example puts the engines, logs, and monitor mode together. It allows outbound traffic only to approved domains and checks that allowed traffic for known threats. The firewall engine holds the domain allow list, and the IPS engine runs the AWS active threat defense managed rule group. Figure 4 shows the policy and where each of the earlier log records comes from. Log record 2 comes from the sample embedded rule, which isn’t part of the policy that you create in the following steps.

Figure 4: The example policy, with the sample embedded rule behind log record 2.

To create the domain list rule group:

In the Network Firewall console, choose Network Firewall rule groups, and then choose Create rule group. Choose Next Generation as the rule group version, Firewall rule group as the type, and Domain list as the format.

Figure 5: Choosing the rule group version, type, and format for the domain list.

Enter one domain per line, for example .amazon.com and checkip.amazonaws.com, and under Protocols, select HTTPS only. For HTTPS, the firewall matches the TLS Server Name Indication (SNI) without decrypting traffic. SNI is the server name that a client sends at the start of a TLS connection. To include a domain and its subdomains, start the name with a dot.

For Capacity sizing, choose Allow room to grow, and then create the rule group.

To create the policy:

Choose Firewall policies, and then choose Create firewall policy. Select Next Generation as the policy version and Drop as the firewall default action, so the firewall blocks traffic that you don’t allow. Set Policy mode to Monitor. We recommend rolling out a new policy in monitor mode first, then switching to enforce after you validate it. Enable Active Threat Defense is selected by default. Active threat defense is optional. Additional charges apply; for details, see AWS Network Firewall pricing.

Figure 6: The policy details page, with Next Generation, Drop, and Monitor selected.

On the Add firewall rule groups step, add the domain list rule group that you created in the previous procedure.

On the Add IPS rule groups step, the active threat defense managed rule group, listed as AttackInfrastructure, is already added. It comes from the Enable Active Threat Defense default that Figure 6 shows. Choose Add rule group to add more AWS managed rule groups, your own rule groups, or embedded rules.

Create the policy, associate it with your firewall, and turn on alert and flow logging.

After you validate the policy, as described in Validate in monitor mode, then enforce, switch Policy mode to Enforce.

For more detail, see Creating a rule group for a Next Generation policy and Generating firewall rules from domain names.

Already using Classic policies?

Classic Network Firewall policies remain supported, and your existing firewalls keep running as they are. Each firewall uses one policy type at a time, either a Classic policy or a Next Generation policy. For new firewalls, we recommend Next Generation policies. We’re working on migration guidance for existing policies, so you can plan a move when it suits you.

To try one now, create a test firewall with a Next Generation policy and start it in monitor mode. To compare the two policy types, see AWS Network Firewall firewall policy versions. Next Generation policies are available at no additional charge. You pay the standard Network Firewall charges for your firewall endpoints and the traffic they process. For Regions and pricing, see AWS Services by Region and AWS Network Firewall pricing.

Conclusion

In this post, we showed you how a Next Generation policy gives access control and threat protection separate engines, each with its own rule capacity, so you can grow your firewall rules and IPS rules independently. We also showed what each engine logs, how to validate a policy in monitor mode, and how to build a policy that allows only approved domains and checks the allowed traffic for threats. To learn more, see Getting started with a Next Generation policy, and to automate your policies, use the AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI) or the AWS SDKs.

If you have questions about this post, contact AWS Support or start a new thread on AWS re:Post.

articles.title: AWS Network Firewall introduces automated internet firewall mode (Preview)
articles.context: For outbound-only connectivity, the firewall first inspects the traffic and then performs NAT, so your rules and logs see each workload’s private IP address
articles.full_text:
AWS Network Firewall now offers automated internet firewall mode (Preview). In this mode, Network Firewall applies your centrally defined rules to traffic at the internet gateway of each of your virtual private clouds (VPCs). It also performs built-in network address translation (NAT) for outbound-only connections. A subnet that reaches the internet needs only one route, directly to the internet gateway. You no longer need to deploy firewall endpoints and NAT gateways in each VPC and configure the routes between them and the subnets. If you’re new to internet traffic inspection, you can start with AWS managed rule groups for Network Firewall. AWS security experts maintain and update these rule groups to help protect your workloads against changing threats. You can deploy these managed rule groups centrally across your environment.

With automated internet firewall mode, you can:

Inspect traffic at the internet gateway – Each VPC gets its own firewall for inbound and outbound IPv4 and IPv6 traffic, with built-in NAT for outbound-only IPv4 connections.

Manage centrally, inspect in each VPC – You define policies in AWS Network Security Manager or start from an AWS managed template. Each VPC’s traffic passes its own firewall, so each VPC you add brings its own inspection capacity. The same central policy also works for VPCs with overlapping Classless Inter-Domain Routing (CIDR) ranges.

Extend coverage to new VPCs – You can create a scope that includes all existing and future VPCs, so your policy applies to new VPCs when teams create them.

In this post, we explain how automated internet firewall mode works and how it fits your existing architecture. We also walk through the steps to deploy it across your environment.

How automated internet firewall mode works

In automated internet firewall mode, Network Firewall applies your rules at the internet gateway of each VPC. Before this launch, inspecting a VPC’s internet traffic meant routing each subnet through a firewall endpoint. Resources that needed outbound-only connectivity also went through a NAT gateway. This mode helps simplify that model by moving inspection to each VPC’s internet gateway. Each subnet now has one route to the internet gateway, where the firewall inspects the traffic and performs built-in NAT (Figure 1).

Figure 1: Outbound traffic before and after automated internet firewall

Each VPC gets its own firewall, not a share of one. When you use VPC endpoint associations to protect multiple VPCs with one firewall, those VPCs share that firewall’s capacity in each Availability Zone. In automated internet firewall mode, each VPC’s firewall supports throughput of up to 100 Gbps in each Availability Zone (Service quotas). It also works when VPCs have overlapping CIDR ranges, because their traffic doesn’t meet in a shared inspection network where the addresses would conflict.

The firewall inspects inbound and outbound traffic. For outbound-only connectivity, the firewall first inspects the traffic and then performs NAT, so your rules and logs see each workload’s private IP address. Built-in NAT translates outbound IPv4 connections from resources without a public IP address, and IPv6 traffic isn’t translated. If your destinations accept only allowlisted source addresses, an Amazon VPC IP Address Manager (IPAM) policy lets you choose the NAT addresses that automated internet firewall mode uses (NAT for outbound traffic).

The firewall uses Network Firewall Next Generation firewall policies. You can start from AWSManagedTemplateIGWFirewallBaseline, an AWS managed template that AWS security experts maintain. You can then add AWS managed rule groups and your own rule groups.

Automated internet firewall mode only inspects traffic that crosses the internet gateway. For traffic between VPCs and to on-premises networks over AWS Direct Connect or AWS Site-to-Site VPN, we recommend a transit gateway-attached Network Firewall.

Subnet connectivity options

Before this launch, a public subnet had a direct route to the internet gateway, and its resources used public IP addresses, so they could connect out and accept inbound connections. A private subnet had no direct route, and its resources reached the internet through a NAT gateway. With automated internet firewall mode, a subnet that reaches the internet can route 0.0.0.0/0 directly to the internet gateway, so the route table no longer separates public from private. Instead, each subnet’s connectivity type decides how its resources reach the internet. You set it in the Network Security Manager policy, not on the subnet. Table 1 maps each type to the model you know.

Connectivity type

Works like

What happens

Flexible (recommended)

A public and a private subnet in one

A resource with a public IP address, such as an Elastic IP address, gets bidirectional access, as in a public subnet. A resource without one gets outbound-only access through built-in NAT, similar to a private subnet.

Bidirectional

A public subnet

Resources with a public IP address connect out and accept inbound connections. Resources without one can’t reach the internet.

Outbound-only

A private IPv4 subnet behind a NAT gateway, or an IPv6 subnet behind an egress-only internet gateway

Unsolicited inbound connections are dropped. Resources without a public IP address connect out through built-in NAT, and resources with one keep their own address.

Excluded

A subnet without a firewall

Traffic bypasses the firewall and built-in NAT.

The firewall inspects traffic in each type except excluded (Figure 2). Each policy sets one default connectivity type for all subnets in scope. You can override it for specific subnets based on tags or on Amazon Resource Name (ARN). When a subnet matches more than one override, the first one in the list applies.

Figure 2: Flexible, bidirectional, and outbound-only subnets are inspected. Excluded subnets aren’t.

Connectivity types also decide which inbound connections reach your resources. The firewall inspects inbound connections to resources with a public IP address in flexible and bidirectional subnets, such as the Network Load Balancer for a non-HTTP service in Figure 3. Figure 3 also shows the outbound path, where instances without a public IP address connect out through the firewall and then built-in NAT. For web applications and APIs, we still recommend AWS WAF on Amazon CloudFront in front of an Application Load Balancer. You can set that load balancer’s subnet to excluded so Network Firewall doesn’t inspect the same request again. Keep in mind that excluded applies in both directions, so any outbound traffic from that subnet also bypasses the firewall.

Figure 3: Inbound and outbound traffic showing inbound, outbound, and excluded connections

Managing automated internet firewall mode

You manage automated internet firewall mode in AWS Network Security Manager. With AWS Organizations, a central security team deploys policies from the Network Security Manager administrator account to the whole organization, to organizational units (OUs), or to specific accounts. Network Security Manager also supports a single-account model, where it applies policies only to that account’s VPCs. You can start from the Network Firewall console or the Network Security Manager console, but the firewall itself is read-only outside Network Security Manager.

Network Security Manager uses three components (Figure 4):

Policy – Combines rules and templates with the connectivity type, enforcement mode, logging, and priority. Rules are the building blocks. A traffic inspection rule decides how the firewall handles traffic, and a firewall configuration rule sets options such as the enforcement mode or logging. A template is an ordered, reusable group of rules, such as AWSManagedTemplateIGWFirewallBaseline, that you can share across policies.

Scope – Selects your organization, OUs, accounts, or VPCs.

Deployment – Binds a policy to a scope. Network Security Manager then creates and manages a firewall in each VPC in scope.

Figure 4: A deployment binds a policy to a scope, and Network Security Manager creates a firewall in each VPC in scope

This model matters most when you manage many VPCs. Because Network Security Manager applies the policy at the internet gateway, the firewall is designed so that VPC owners and subnet owners without the proper privileges can’t bypass inspection by changing routes. Subnets set to excluded and Availability Zones where automated internet firewall mode isn’t supported aren’t inspected.

Many organizations want one security baseline everywhere, while some accounts, organizational units, or applications need rules in addition to the baseline. To do this, you create two policies, each deployed to its own scope. The organization policy holds a baseline template, and the Account A policy holds the same baseline template plus Account A’s rules (Figure 5). The template lets you maintain the baseline rules once and reuse them in both policies. Where policies overlap, the policy with the lower priority number applies in full, and the policies don’t merge. In Account A, the Account A policy (priority 100) wins over the organization policy (priority 1000), so it must include the baseline template. Its enforcement mode, logging, and connectivity type also replace the organization policy’s. To learn more, see How AWS Network Security Manager works.

Figure 5: The Account A policy, priority 100, takes priority in Account A. Other accounts get the organization policy, priority 1000.

Getting started

We recommend starting in monitor mode, especially in VPCs with existing workloads. In monitor mode, the firewall logs what your rules would do but doesn’t drop traffic because of them. After the logs show the results you expect, switch the policy to enforce. In this example, we create a policy in monitor mode in six steps.

Start from the AWS Management Console for Network Firewall. On the Firewalls page, open the Internet firewalls tab and choose Create in AWS Network Security Manager. The Quick create and deploy page opens in the Network Security Manager console. Select Network Firewall automated internet firewall as the firewall type.

Figure 6: Create a new internet firewall

Define protections. Choose Manage templates and add AWSManagedTemplateIGWFirewallBaseline. Under Enforcement mode, select Monitor, and choose destinations for alert logs and flow logs.

Figure 7: Define protections and set destinations for logs

Enter a name for the policy and check its Policy priority. Where policies overlap, the lower number takes priority. The new policy gets a priority that evaluates after your existing policies of the same firewall type, and you can change it later in the policy editor.

Figure 8: Set the policy details

Set the scope. For example, you can set the scope for Accounts and OUs to include the entire organization and the scope for VPCs to include all existing and future VPCs. To learn more about scopes, see How AWS Network Security Manager works.

Figure 9: Set the scope

Choose the Subnet connectivity type. For example, select Flex (recommended).

Figure 10: Choose the subnet connectivity type

Review your settings and choose Create and deploy. Cross-account visibility lets Network Security Manager see resources in the accounts in the scope.

Figure 11: Review and deploy

Network Security Manager then creates a firewall at the internet gateway of each VPC in scope. For the full steps, including the organization baseline with account-specific rules, see Getting started with automated internet firewall.

Migrating existing VPCs to automated internet firewall mode

When you deploy automated internet firewall mode to an existing VPC, you might not need to change routes on day one. With the flexible type, the firewall inspects existing resources and keeps the addresses they already use (Figure 12):

Instance with an Elastic IP address – The firewall inspects its traffic, and the instance keeps its Elastic IP address.

Instance behind a NAT gateway – The firewall inspects the traffic after the NAT gateway translates it and doesn’t translate it again. Your rules and logs see the NAT gateway’s private IP address as the source.

Instance with no public IP address in a subnet that routes to the internet gateway – The firewall inspects its traffic, and built-in NAT gives it outbound-only access, which it didn’t have before. To keep resources without a public IP address isolated from the internet, set the subnet’s connectivity type to bidirectional instead. Resources with a public IP address then keep bidirectional connectivity, and resources without one can’t reach the internet.

Figure 12: Day-one source addresses in an existing VPC with Flexible subnets

Later, at your own pace, you can retire each NAT gateway by routing its subnets directly to the internet gateway. Built-in NAT then takes over. The source address changes to one that automated internet firewall mode assigns or one from your IPAM policy pool, so update allow lists that name the NAT gateway’s address first. Your logs then show each workload’s private IP address. If you inspect inbound or outbound internet traffic today with Network Firewall endpoints, automated internet firewall mode can take over that inspection. After you confirm that your new policy covers the same rules, you can remove the endpoints and routes that you use for internet traffic. For each architecture, see Working with existing architectures.

Availability and pricing

Automated internet firewall mode (Preview) is available in all AWS commercial Regions. For pricing, see AWS Network Firewall pricing. During the preview, some features and instance types aren’t supported. For the list, see Automated internet firewall. Features, service quotas, and console labels can change during the preview. Your use of the preview is subject to the Betas and Previews section of the AWS Service Terms.

Conclusion

In this post, we showed you how automated internet firewall mode applies Network Firewall inspection and built-in NAT at the internet gateway of your VPCs. You define and control policies centrally in Network Security Manager. It is designed so that VPC owners without the proper privileges can’t route around it, and your policy applies to new VPCs in scope when teams create them. To learn more, see Automated internet firewall in the Network Firewall Developer Guide.

If you have questions about this post, contact AWS Support or start a new thread on AWS re:Post.

He’s focused on making virtual private clouds more intuitive and secure for the millions of customers running their workloads on AWS. articles.title: Introducing AWS WAF simplified pricing
articles.context: Until then, you keep your current pricing, and you don’t need to do anything at launch
articles.full_text:
Starting today, AWS WAF pricing is easier to predict. Your bill is now based on three dimensions: the resources you protect, the traffic AWS WAF inspects, and the level of protection you apply to that traffic.

Existing AWS WAF customers move to the new pricing on February 1, 2027. Until then, you keep your current pricing, and you don’t need to do anything at launch. This post explains what’s changing, how to estimate your costs under the new model, and where to find full pricing details and examples on the AWS WAF pricing page.

For new or smaller workloads, the Free plan of CloudFront flat-rate pricing plans is another way to start. If your application serves fewer than 1 million requests per month, the Free plan costs $0 per month for each CloudFront distribution. It includes AWS WAF protection against common web threats, DDoS protection, and the CloudFront CDN, with no overage charges.

Why the pricing is changing

Under the previous model, adding a protection often meant adding a charge, so every security decision was also a billing decision. The new pricing separates those two questions and makes the trade off between cost and security posture easy to see. Turning on a rule, the Bot Control common protection, or the Anti-DDoS rule group doesn’t add a subscription or a separate per-request charge. Those requests bill at the base request rate.

Capacity also stops affecting your rate. Each protection pack (web ACL) now includes up to 2,500 web ACL capacity units (WCUs), up from 1,500, and going past your included capacity no longer raises what you pay per request. The premium request fee applies only to the traffic you choose to send through advanced protections.

You can estimate costs before writing a single rule, and those estimates hold even as your rules change. Security rules change often. A new CVE or a shift in bot behavior can require a configuration update the same day. Adding, reordering, or removing rules doesn’t change your rate.

What this means for existing customers

If you already use AWS WAF, your account stays on current pricing until February 1, 2027. If you hold an AWS WAF private pricing agreement, it stays in force until it expires.

You don’t have to work out the math yourself. The AWS WAF pricing page includes worked examples that show how the three fees add up for common workloads. If you have questions about how the new pricing applies to your account, contact your AWS account team or open a Support case.

For AWS Shield Advanced subscribers, nothing changes. Your Shield Advanced subscription, its price, and your included AWS WAF entitlement stay the same. AWS WAF remains included up to 1,500 WCU per protection pack (web ACL), the resources Shield Advanced protects stay unmetered, and AWS WAF base requests remain free up to 50 billion per calendar month.

Customers on a CloudFront flat-rate pricing plan also see no change. AWS WAF stays included in your plan, and your plan’s included requests stay the same.

How the new pricing works

AWS WAF bills three fees. The resource fee is an hourly charge for each resource associated with a protection pack (web ACL). It covers resources that AWS WAF can protect, such as Amazon CloudFront distributions, Application Load Balancers, and Amazon API Gateway APIs. The base request fee applies to each request AWS WAF inspects. The premium request fee applies on top of the base request fee, to the requests that advanced protections evaluate, such as Bot Control targeted protections, Fraud Control, API Security, and AI Security. AWS WAF also launches two new managed rule groups today, API Security and AI Security. Both use the same premium request fee, with no separate subscription or rate. For the current list of advanced protections, see the AWS WAF Developer Guide.

Fee

What it’s charged for

Rate

Resource fee

Each resource associated with a protection pack (web ACL), prorated hourly

$0.01 per hour (about $7.30 per month)

Base request fee

Each request that AWS WAF inspects

$0.60 per million requests

Premium request fee

Requests evaluated by advanced protections, in addition to the base request fee

$5.00 per million requests

Requests evaluated by one or more advanced protections are billed $5.60 per million: the $0.60 base request fee plus the $5.00 premium request fee. AWS WAF charges the premium request fee once per request, however many advanced protections evaluate it. A request that Bot Control targeted protections, API Security, and AI Security evaluate is still billed $5.60 per million. A request that an earlier rule blocks before it reaches an advanced protection pays only the base request fee. For instance, a request blocked by a custom rule before it reaches Bot Control pays $0.60 per million, not $5.60.

Figure 1 shows where each previous charge lands under the new pricing model. AWS WAF also inspects request bodies up to the maximum size that each associated resource type supports, at no extra charge. For the current limits by resource type, see Considerations for managing body inspection in AWS WAF.

Figure 1: Mapping of previous AWS WAF pricing components to the new three-dimension model

See your traffic with the Security analytics dashboard

The new pricing also includes the Security analytics dashboard. The dashboard shows full traffic metrics for your protected applications over a rolling 21 day window. You can use it to see the requests your protection packs (web ACLs) inspect and how your rules act on them, which helps you tune the protections and understand what drives your request fees. The dashboard is included at no additional cost.

Estimating your bill

Figure 2 shows how the three dimensions add up for three example workloads.

Example 1: One protected resource. One Application Load Balancer serving 20 million requests per month.

Resource fee: 1 resource × $0.01 per hour × 730 hours = $7.30

Base request fee: 20 million × $0.60 per million = $12.00

Total: $19.30 per month

Example 2: A larger footprint. 40 resources serving 150 million requests per month.

Resource fee: 40 × $7.30 = $292.00

Base request fee: 150 million × $0.60 per million = $90.00

Total: $382.00 per month. At this size, the resource fee is the larger share.

Example 3: Advanced protections. 5 resources, 300 million requests, 30 million of them evaluated by advanced protections.

Resource fee: 5 × $7.30 = $36.50

Base request fee: 300 million × $0.60 per million = $180.00

Premium request fee: 30 million × $5.00 per million = $150.00

Total: $366.50 per month

Figure 2: How the three dimensions add up for three example workloads

To estimate your own bill, start with how many resources each protection pack (web ACL) is associated with, since that drives the resource fee. For request volumes, AWS WAF publishes Amazon CloudWatch metrics for each protection pack (web ACL) and each protected resource, including the requests your advanced protections evaluate. The Security analytics dashboard gives you the same traffic view without building your own reports.

A few architectural choices can also help. Where it fits your architecture, protecting traffic at Amazon CloudFront can cost less than protecting many downstream resources one by one. If you serve many customer domains, Amazon CloudFront SaaS Manager lets you manage them as tenants of one multi-tenant distribution, so you can apply one protection pack across them. Scope-down statements send advanced protections only the traffic that warrants them, such as login or checkout paths.

Availability and getting started

The new AWS WAF pricing is available starting today. To get started, open the AWS WAF console, review your protection packs (web ACLs) and their resource associations, and review the examples on the AWS WAF pricing page.

Frequently asked questions

Does AWS WAF charge for requests it blocks? Yes. AWS WAF bills each request it inspects, including the requests it blocks. The protected resource bills those requests as usual, except Amazon CloudFront, which doesn’t charge for requests that AWS WAF blocks (learn more).

If a request passes through two protection packs (web ACLs), is it billed twice? Yes. For example, if a request passes a protection pack (web ACL) on a CloudFront distribution and another on the Application Load Balancer behind it, each protection pack (web ACL) bills it.

Does the Security analytics dashboard cost extra? No. The dashboard is included with AWS WAF at no additional cost.

Does pricing change for AWS Marketplace managed rule groups or AWS Shield Advanced? No. Pricing for AWS Marketplace managed rule groups and AWS Shield Advanced stays the same, and resources protected by Shield Advanced stay on their current pricing.

Is there a free tier? AWS WAF does not have a standalone free tier. If you serve your application through CloudFront and it handles fewer than 1 million requests per month, the CloudFront flat-rate Free plan includes AWS WAF at $0 per month. For plan details, see CloudFront flat-rate pricing plans.

What if my application needs more than 2,500 WCU? Open an AWS Support case to request a capacity increase.

Conclusion

The new AWS WAF pricing makes cost easier to plan around, so it does not become a blocker to security best practices. Your bill follows three things you can measure: the resources you protect, the requests AWS WAF inspects, and the requests that advanced protections evaluate. Adding, changing, or reordering rules doesn’t change your rate, and turning on Bot Control common protections or the Anti-DDoS rule group doesn’t add a subscription. The Security analytics dashboard gives you 21 days of traffic visibility at no additional cost.

To see what the change means for you, review the examples on the AWS WAF pricing page, or model a new workload in the AWS Pricing Calculator.

If you have questions about this post, contact AWS Support or start a new thread on AWS re:Post.
