articles.title: Introducing API and AI security on AWS, from discovery to protection
articles.context: So a detection reaches high confidence only when different kinds of signs agree, and at least one is something your own traffic never does
articles.full_text:
APIs have run digital businesses for more than a decade. For a while, there seemed to be nothing new left to say about them. That changed in 2026, when AI endpoints joined them. Teams now run large language model (LLM) inference endpoints, Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers, and Agent2Agent (A2A) servers beside their REST APIs, on services such as Amazon Bedrock, Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, and Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS), and more companies sell their API as the product itself. On the other end, AI agents read API descriptions, pick the tools they need, and chain calls with no person clicking through an app.

APIs have always had two kinds of callers: other services and people who use an app. Now there’s a third: AI agents that act on a person’s behalf. It feels like everyone has a personal AI agent that can call APIs for them. Who knew curl would be important again?

Today, we’re launching capabilities across AWS WAF, Amazon CloudFront, Application Load Balancer, and Amazon API Gateway that help you discover and protect the APIs and AI endpoints that services, apps, and AI agents call:

API Portal, a new feature in Amazon API Gateway, discovers your APIs and AI endpoints.

API Security, a new managed rule group in AWS WAF, protects your APIs.

AI Security, a new managed rule group in AWS WAF, protects your AI endpoints.

All three are generally available today. You can enable discovery in API Portal for one account or for your organization in AWS Organizations. The two rule groups protect the resources that you associate with your protection pack (web ACL). They work together: API Portal shows which discovered endpoints AWS WAF protects, and the security events that AWS WAF detects appear on each managed API’s detail page.

Same APIs, new callers, new attack surface

Your APIs are the same APIs they always were. What changed is how you expose them, who calls them, and what threatens them.

How you expose them. A new MCP server or LLM endpoint takes minutes to stand up. It can be placed behind a load balancer or a CloudFront distribution without ever passing through your API gateway, so it’s missing from the API registry and the security review. An agent that can reach it doesn’t need your documentation, either, because the endpoint describes itself: an MCP client asks the server for its tools with tools/list, and an A2A client reads the agent card that the server publishes.

Who calls them. The following table compares the three kinds of callers that reach your APIs today.

Caller

What normal looks like

What abuse looks like

What it means for protection

Service to service

Predictable, authenticated calls that repeat the same pattern

A stolen API key, or a partner that scrapes beyond its contract

Track rate and behavior for each API key and endpoint

Person to service, through an app

Sessions and UI-driven calls at a human pace

Account takeover and scripted checkouts

Browser-based signals, such as CAPTCHA and browser fingerprints, apply here

AI agent to service, for a person

Human intent with machine behavior, from an HTTP client or an automated browser

An agent with stolen credentials, or a bot that poses as an agent

Browser signals only go so far, so you need visibility into the API itself

What threatens them. The APIs behind your web and mobile apps were built for one client: your own app. Your app calls them in the right order, at a human pace, with input it already validated. Legitimate agents now call those same APIs directly, and so do attackers and fraudsters. None of them have to follow the rules that your app follows.

What we’re launching

Here’s how we respond to those changes, as shown in Figure 1. In the figure, services, people, and AI agents call your APIs through their entry points. There, API Portal maps your endpoints, and AWS WAF runs API Security and AI Security on the same traffic to stop threats.

Figure 1: API Portal inventories the APIs and AI endpoints that services, people, and AI agents call. AWS WAF protects the entry points in front of them

API Portal builds an inventory of your APIs from their configuration and live traffic, identifies which of them are AI endpoints (LLM inference, MCP, and A2A), and shows you what to protect. It does this by analyzing configuration and traffic across your API entry points: CloudFront, Application Load Balancer, and API Gateway.

API Security covers three kinds of API abuse: broken object level authorization, authentication attacks such as tampered tokens and credential stuffing, and reconnaissance such as probing for undocumented routes. It does this with rules that work from a single request and with behavioral detections that learn your traffic.

AI Security identifies your AI traffic (LLM inference, MCP, and A2A), validates MCP and A2A requests against their protocol, and checks prompts and responses through Amazon Bedrock Guardrails for prompt attacks, harmful content, and sensitive information.

All three work with Amazon CloudFront, Amazon API Gateway REST APIs, and Application Load Balancer. For the current list of supported resources, protocols, and endpoint types, see AWS WAF API Security and AWS WAF AI Security rule group in the AWS WAF Developer Guide.

The three capabilities live in two places. API Portal is in the Amazon API Gateway console. That’s where it can be found, not what it covers: it discovers APIs behind CloudFront, Application Load Balancer, and API Gateway alike. API Security and AI Security are in the AWS WAF console.

Discover: You can’t secure an invisible API

Ask a platform team how many APIs they run, and you’ll get a number from a registry. Ask what’s answering requests on the internet right now, and the number changes. The MCP server that a team set up for a hackathon isn’t in the registry. Neither is the v1 endpoint that nobody turned off. Both still answer requests.

API Portal builds the inventory from both live traffic and API configuration. You enable discovery in API Portal for one account or for your organization in AWS Organizations, and you can exclude resources that you don’t want in the inventory. It reads the service logs and configuration records of your API entry points. There’s nothing to attach, no logs to forward, and no traffic to reroute. It lists the endpoints that receive traffic, by host, path, and HTTP method. Every endpoint starts as a shadow API: deployed and reachable, but not yet governed. When you promote it, it becomes a managed API. For APIs you manage, API Portal also flags zombie APIs, which have no traffic and no configuration change for a set period, and orphaned APIs, whose owning account was closed or removed from your organization. Retire a zombie API that nothing needs, and resolve the ownership of an orphaned one. For the classification rules, see the API Portal Developer Guide.

API Portal also discovers your AI endpoints. It reports each endpoint’s type, such as an LLM inference endpoint, an MCP server, or an A2A server. It finds them in the traffic at the same entry points (CloudFront, Application Load Balancer, and API Gateway) and lists them in the same inventory as your other APIs, so you don’t build a separate view for them. Combined, one row can show a shadow MCP server that nobody manages yet. Figure 2 shows the inventory.

Figure 2: The API inventory in API Portal lists the endpoints discovered behind API Gateway and Application Load Balancer, with each endpoint’s AWS WAF status, classification, and AI workload type

“We can manage our API environment more effectively when we have a clear picture of what’s running across AWS. API Portal gives us that visibility without requiring teams to change how they deploy APIs or route traffic, helping us create a more complete view across the enterprise.” — Mike Hasani, Senior Software Engineer, Principal Financial Group

Some abuse shows in one request. Some appears only over time.

Two requests show why protecting an API takes two kinds of detection. Here’s the first one:

GET /v1/orders/48213 HTTP/1.1 Host: orders.example.com Authorization: Bearer eyJhbGciOiJub25lIiwidHlwIjoiSldUIn0.eyJzdWIiOiJhZG1pbiIsInJvbGUiOiJhZG1pbiJ9.

This JSON Web Token (JWT) declares alg: none. It asks your API to skip signature verification, and a correctly built client doesn’t send that. The API Security managed rule group blocks the request before it reaches your origin, from the first request and with no learning period. The same rules catch other token tampering, such as pointing the token at a signing key that the attacker controls. These rules check the structure of a token in the Authorization header. They don’t verify its signature, so your application still has to validate the token. For the full list of rules and what each one does by default, see API Security managed rule group in the AWS WAF Developer Guide.

Here’s the second one:

GET /accounts/1337 HTTP/1.1

Nothing is wrong with this request, and the caller’s token is valid. It’s abuse only if the caller doesn’t own account 1337, and no single request can tell you that. This is broken object level authorization (BOLA), the first entry in the OWASP API Security Top 10.

So, the managed rule group also learns. It builds a baseline from your own traffic and looks for callers who don’t fit it. There’s nothing to set up for this. You don’t turn on logging or mirror traffic.

The hard part is to avoid flagging your own scripts. For example, a nightly export job reads thousands of records on a steady machine schedule. On those two signs alone, it looks like an attacker. So a detection reaches high confidence only when different kinds of signs agree, and at least one is something your own traffic never does. For example, the caller reaches records through a sequence of calls that your app never makes, or your API keeps denying it access. High confidence also needs a caller that AWS WAF can identify from a credential on the request, such as a token. A caller that AWS WAF knows only by IP address stays at medium confidence. Figure 3 compares a nightly export job with an attacker on these signs.

Figure 3: Volume and timing alone don’t reach high confidence. A sign that your own traffic never shows has to agree with them

The behavioral detections cover more than object access. They also flag credential stuffing, where one source presents an unusual number of different credentials in the Authorization header, and probing, where a caller keeps requesting routes or parameters that your traffic never uses.

The same thinking applies to the response, what your APIs send back. The behavioral detections take account of the status codes that your application returns, such as a caller’s rate of denied or failed requests. A caller stands out when, for example, its successful calls turn into a run of authorization failures. API Security doesn’t inspect the content of responses. Figure 4 shows the APIs view of the protection pack (web ACL) dashboard in the AWS WAF console.

Figure 4: The APIs view of the protection pack (web ACL) dashboard shows API Security detections over time, the detections that matched the most requests, and how AWS WAF handled the labeled requests.

Every detection is a label under awswaf:managed:aws:api-security:. A label starts with a stage (attack, recon, or warning) and names the finding. Behavioral detections also end with a confidence (high, medium, or low). Each rule has its own default action. The single-request rules that identify token tampering and unsafe methods block, and the posture and schema discovery rules count. Behavioral detections block at high confidence and count at medium and low confidence, at either stage. Detections that work from a single request have no confidence. For example, attack:alg_none:jwt_header and attack:object_level:high block, and recon:path_schema counts. AWS WAF also repeats a caller’s finding as an actor_identity label on that caller’s later requests across the whole protection pack (web ACL), for about five minutes after the last detection. At high confidence, the rule group blocks those requests by default. At medium and low confidence it counts them, and your own rules can act on the label.

AI Security understands the protocols that agents speak

LLM inference endpoints, MCP servers, and A2A servers are APIs, too. API Portal shows you which of your endpoints they are, and the API Security managed rule group already inspects their requests like any other API path.

The AI Security managed rule group adds checks made for agent traffic. It first recognizes the traffic and labels each request as LLM, MCP, A2A, or not recognized, so the checks that follow fit each endpoint type. It runs in the same AWS WAF protection pack (web ACL) as your other rules, with no new service to deploy.

Its first layer checks each MCP and A2A request against the protocol version that the request declares in its MCP-Protocol-Version or A2A-Version header. It supports MCP versions 2025-06-18, 2025-11-25, and 2026-07-28, and A2A version 1.0. For the current list, see AI Security managed rule group. These protocol compliance checks are deterministic and run entirely in AWS WAF. They come in two levels. Baseline covers the violations that let a request slip past routing or inspection, as the example that follows shows, and blocks by default. Strict adds malformed requests that are worth flagging but are usually an outdated client, and counts by default. Each failed check also adds its own label, so you can see exactly which check failed. Here’s the kind of trick that Baseline catches. The header tells every component in front of the MCP server that the request only lists tools. The body calls a tool that reads a file:

POST /mcp HTTP/1.1 Host: tools.example.com Content-Type: application/json MCP-Protocol-Version: 2026-07-28 Mcp-Method: tools/list Mcp-Name: read_file { "jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 1, "method": "tools/call", "params": { "name": "read_file", "arguments": { "path": "/etc/passwd" } } }

A gateway or authorizer that trusts the header treats the request as read-only, and the server runs the tool. AWS WAF blocks the request at the API entry point, because the header and the body disagree about the method.

Its second layer checks content through Amazon Bedrock Guardrails. You don’t create or configure a guardrail for this. You turn on the option in the rule group and choose a service role, and AWS WAF assumes that role to call Bedrock Guardrails with your account’s identity. Bedrock Guardrails returns a score for each check. AWS WAF groups the scores into three levels (high, medium, and low), and the rule group has one rule for each check at each level, so you choose the action for each one. AWS WAF picks the checks for each endpoint type and each direction, as the following table shows. Response checks run only when you turn on response inspection. They cover the response body up to the body size that AWS WAF inspects for that resource, and content beyond that size isn’t checked.

Bedrock Guardrails check

What it looks for

On requests

On responses

Prompt attack

Jailbreaks, prompt injection, and attempts to extract the system prompt

Yes

MCP and A2A only

Content filter

Hate, insults, sexual content, violence, and misconduct

LLM and A2A only

No

Sensitive information

Personal data such as card numbers, US Social Security numbers, email addresses, and bank account numbers, plus credentials such as passwords and AWS access keys

No

Yes

By default, AWS WAF blocks a high-severity prompt attack, on the request or the response. Everything else counts and adds a label that names what matched, such as a prompt injection or a card number. You can change the action for any rule. If Bedrock Guardrails can’t check a request, AWS WAF adds a label that says why and lets the request through. The label is guardrails:not_assessed when the content can’t be assessed, such as an empty prompt. It’s guardrails:call_failed when the call to Bedrock Guardrails fails, plus a second label with the reason, such as guardrails:call_failed:throttling. Like every label, these appear in your AWS WAF logs and CloudWatch metrics. For how labels work, see Web request labeling in AWS WAF. To fail closed when the call to Bedrock Guardrails fails, set the Guardrails_CallFailed rule to block. Throttling then blocks requests, too. Content checks run in the supported Regions listed in AWS WAF AI Security rule group. Figure 5 follows one request through these checks.

Figure 5: AWS WAF recognizes agent traffic and checks its protocol itself, and calls Amazon Bedrock Guardrails to check the prompt on the way in and the answer on the way out

The AI Security labels follow the same steps, under awswaf:managed:aws:ai-security:. For example, traffic:recognized_mcp says what the traffic is, protocol_compliance_level:baseline:mcp is the level you act on, protocol_compliance_check:mcp_method_mismatch names the check that failed, and request:guardrails:prompt_attack:severity:high carries the Bedrock Guardrails result. For the full label list, supported protocols, and configuration, see AI Security managed rule group. Figure 6 shows the AI endpoints view of the protection pack (web ACL) dashboard.

Figure 6: The AI endpoints view of the protection pack (web ACL) dashboard shows AI Security detections over time, the Amazon Bedrock Guardrails findings that matched the most requests, and how AWS WAF handled AI traffic

Every detection is a label, and labels work with the rest of AWS WAF

Every detection from the API Security and AI Security rule groups is also a label on the request. Any rule that runs later in your protection pack can match those labels and combine them with labels from other managed rule groups. Examples are AWS WAF Bot Control, AWS WAF Fraud Control account takeover prevention, and the Amazon IP reputation list. That list draws on MadPot, the threat intelligence tool that Amazon uses to protect customers from cybercrime. Use request labels in your own rules. Labels from response checks, such as sensitive information in a response, drive the AI Security rule group’s own actions and appear in your CloudWatch metrics.

Here are four examples of what that makes possible:

Rate limits keyed on labels. One probe for your API schema can be noise. Fifty from the same caller in 5 minutes is reconnaissance. A rate-based rule scoped to the reconnaissance labels counts only those requests.

No unsigned agents on your MCP server. If your MCP server is only for agents you work with, block requests without an access token or a verified Web Bot Auth signature. Then match the Bot Control bot name label for the operators you trust. Application Load Balancer JWT verification, CloudFront Functions, Lambda@Edge, or your MCP server still validates the token itself.

Two weak signals that add up. A low-confidence API Security label or a Bot Control signal by itself isn’t enough to block. Block only the requests that carry both.

Tighter limits on sensitive paths. Bot Control targeted protection labels callers by confidence. Use those labels to set a lower rate limit on /checkout than on the rest of your API.

The following rule shows the first example. For each IP address, it counts the requests that carry an API Security reconnaissance label. When an address sends more than 50 requests in 5 minutes, the rule blocks them. Place it after the API Security managed rule group so that its labels are available.

{ "Name": "RateLimitAPISecurityRecon", "Priority": 40, "Statement": { "RateBasedStatement": { "Limit": 50, "EvaluationWindowSec": 300, "AggregateKeyType": "IP", "ScopeDownStatement": { "LabelMatchStatement": { "Scope": "NAMESPACE", "Key": "awswaf:managed:aws:api-security:recon:" } } } }, "Action": { "Block": {} }, "VisibilityConfig": { "SampledRequestsEnabled": true, "CloudWatchMetricsEnabled": true, "MetricName": "RateLimitAPISecurityRecon" } }

Labels don’t have to stop at AWS WAF. With custom request headers and dynamic label interpolation, AWS WAF can forward the matched labels to your origin. Your application then sees what AWS WAF saw and can show less data, require step-up authentication, or log the request for review. For how it works, see Do more with AWS WAF labels using dynamic label interpolation.

We keep adding labels, so the documentation holds the current lists. See API Security labels, AI Security labels, and AWS WAF Bot Control rule group.

See what the rule groups found, and act on it

Every label is also an Amazon CloudWatch metric, with no extra setup, and appears in your AWS WAF logs. The protection pack (web ACL) dashboard in the AWS WAF console shows them as traffic arrives. In API Portal, each managed API’s detail page shows the security events that AWS WAF detected on it, as shown in Figure 7.

Figure 7: Each managed API’s detail page in API Portal shows the events that AWS WAF detected on it

The managed rule groups enforce their own detections at your API entry points. To write a rule of your own, start from a label. Scope a rate-based rule to the paths it appears on, key it on the IP address or TLS fingerprint, and start in count mode.

When a detection type spikes, your existing alerting can act on it. That can be a CloudWatch alarm, or the observability or security platform that already reads your metrics and logs. For log destinations, see Logging AWS WAF protection pack (web ACL) traffic.

How we test API Security

No single test shows whether a detection works, so we combine several for API Security:

Automated red teaming – LLM-powered agents run continuously against deliberately vulnerable test APIs that we maintain. They probe, adapt, and chain steps the way an attacker does.

A growing attack suite – Each working exploit that the agents find becomes a repeatable test case. We replay the suite against the managed rule group when it changes.

Realistic legitimate traffic – We replay traffic such as batch jobs, seasonal spikes, and power users next to the attacks, so we measure false positives together with detections.

Results from our test environment don’t transfer directly to yours, because your APIs and the attacks against them differ. The numbers that matter come from your own traffic, and the next section shows how to get them. API Security is designed to detect and block callers who walk object IDs to harvest other users’ records, and tokens whose structure shows tampering. It also flags credential stuffing against the Authorization header and callers who probe for routes that your API doesn’t serve. Efficacy and expansion work for API Security, like AWS WAF security in general, is a continuous effort. For the current list of detections, see API Security managed rule group in the AWS WAF Developer Guide.

Check what gets blocked on your own traffic

The managed rule groups apply their default actions from the moment you add them. To see what a rule group finds before it blocks anything, first add it with all rule actions overridden to count, review the results, and then remove the override. Later, to review one rule, override only that rule to count. AWS WAF still evaluates an overridden rule and adds its label, so you see what it would have blocked on your own production traffic.

Behavioral detections need time to learn your traffic. For the learning period, see Testing and deploying AWS WAF API Security. For a step-by-step evaluation, see Testing and tuning your AWS WAF protections.

Availability

API Portal, API Security, and AI Security are generally available today. Detection of data exfiltration and sensitive data exposure in responses for API Security is coming soon.

Pricing

Each capability is priced by the service it runs in. For API Portal, see Amazon API Gateway pricing. For the API Security and AI Security managed rule groups, see AWS WAF pricing. For the content checks that AI Security runs through Bedrock Guardrails, see Amazon Bedrock pricing.

Get started

To get started, complete the following steps:

In API Portal, enable discovery for one account or for your organization in AWS Organizations, and exclude any resources that you don’t want in the inventory. This step doesn’t need AWS WAF. As the inventory builds, look for endpoints you didn’t expect, such as shadow APIs and AI endpoints, and add them to your managed APIs.

In the AWS WAF console, add the API Security managed rule group to the protection pack in front of your APIs. Start with all rule actions overridden to count, review what it finds on your own traffic, and then remove the override.

If you run AI endpoints, add the AI Security managed rule group to the same protection pack. To turn on the Bedrock Guardrails checks, choose a service role that AWS WAF can assume to call Bedrock Guardrails, and turn on response inspection if you want responses checked and your protection pack (web ACL) protects CloudFront or an Application Load Balancer. Start with the four rules that block by default overridden to count, review what they find on your own traffic, and then remove the overrides one rule at a time.

After the first baseline is available, the behavioral detections label abuse and block it at high confidence. Watch the labels in your CloudWatch metrics, and in your AWS WAF logs if you turn on logging.

Use those labels in your own rules, such as a lower rate limit on your most sensitive paths.

For step-by-step instructions, see Adding the API Security managed rule group and Adding the AI Security managed rule group in the AWS WAF Developer Guide.

Best practice: Put Amazon CloudFront in front of your APIs

Put Amazon CloudFront in front of your API Gateway APIs, your Application Load Balancers, and any other endpoint that is public on port 80 or 443, and associate your protection pack (web ACL) with the CloudFront distribution. That includes APIs that run outside AWS, with another cloud provider or on premises: CloudFront works with any HTTP or HTTPS origin, so those APIs get the same delivery, acceleration, and protection. The same applies to your MCP servers, A2A servers, and LLM endpoints, whether you host them on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway, on Amazon EKS, or elsewhere. With this setup:

AWS WAF inspects requests at the edge, before they reach your origin.

AWS WAF sees the caller’s own IP address.

AWS WAF mitigates attacks close to their source.

For origins in AWS, CloudFront VPC origins mean your Application Load Balancer or private API Gateway REST API isn’t exposed directly to the public internet and is reached through CloudFront.

For more information, see Use AWS WAF protections and Restrict access with VPC origins in the Amazon CloudFront Developer Guide, and the posts Introducing Amazon CloudFront VPC origins and Accessing private Amazon API Gateway endpoints through custom Amazon CloudFront distribution using VPC Origins.

Conclusion

Your APIs are the same APIs they always were. The callers changed, and so did the attack surface. With API Portal, you can see the APIs and AI endpoints that the internet is calling. With API Security and AI Security in AWS WAF, you can protect them at their entry points, without changes to your backend code.

AWS built the building blocks for what comes next: an inventory from traffic, labels that you can act on, and protection where requests first arrive. As agents and the protocols they speak change, those building blocks are where new protection shows up. For the most up-to-date information, see AWS WAF API Security and AWS WAF AI Security in the AWS WAF Developer Guide.

To get started, enable discovery in API Portal, and add the API Security and AI Security managed rule groups in the AWS WAF console.

Now, we're opening up EFS in public beta. In this post, we explain how EFS works in more detail, how it stays compatible with ZDR, and how businesses can join the beta program.

How EFS provides automated safety monitoring with ZDR

Customers who rely on legacy ZDR are protected by Claude's classifiers: our real-time safeguards that screen individual requests to assess whether they might cause harm. But sophisticated attacks generally occur across multiple queries—and any single request might, in isolation, look harmless.

For example, our September threat intelligence report describes an operation against roughly fifty organizations in which an AI agent divided the work of an attack among many other agents running in parallel. It saved the credentials it had harvested between sessions, so that the attackers could easily resume their campaign. Viewed one request at a time, this attack would have appeared as separate, more benign tasks.

To catch attacks like these, we use a second defensive layer, known as automated safety monitoring. This layer looks for patterns of misuse across many requests. Through EFS, Anthropic can provide automated safety monitoring without storing any customer data. Instead, our automated safety monitoring system analyzes data stored entirely on infrastructure controlled by our customers.

When automated safety monitoring finds a risk, it creates a Safety Case for you to review. These cases can be read from your cloud storage or through an API, and can be integrated with security information and event management systems. They do not include inputs and outputs.

Once it's set up, automated safety monitoring can help your team detect intentional misuse that could lead to serious harm (like offensive cyber operations). It can also help detect agents that take actions beyond a user's intentions, such as—in extreme cases—using a software exploit to access an internal database or external system.

Zero data retention and EFS

With EFS, you bring your own storage for storing inputs and outputs. Neither Anthropic nor your cloud provider keeps a copy of your data once it is delivered to storage you control. This provides you the following guarantees:

Zero data retention. Neither Anthropic nor your cloud provider retains your data. You bring your own storage and store your own data. Inputs and outputs are deleted promptly after they're written to your own storage. You configure your own access policies and audit logging, and encrypt safety data with your own keys.

No operator human review. Neither Anthropic nor your cloud provider personnel access your inputs and outputs. Only automated safety monitoring can access this data.

We never train on your data. Inputs and outputs are used only for automated safety monitoring, never for model or classifier training.

You can use EFS through the Claude Platform, Claude Platform on AWS, Amazon Bedrock, or Claude on Google Cloud. When you use EFS through Amazon Bedrock or Claude on Google Cloud (Google Managed), it's operated by your cloud provider, and the end-to-end data flow stays within that cloud's boundary.

You can use Amazon S3 or Google Cloud Storage in your own account for your storage, depending on where you use Claude. Your cloud provider bills you for that storage as usual, including reads, writes, and key operations (plus any applicable network transfer).

Get started

EFS is available on the Claude Platform, Claude Platform on AWS, Amazon Bedrock, and Claude on Google Cloud. Support for EFS in Microsoft Foundry is coming soon.

Eligible customers will be notified with instructions on how to get started. Read our developer docs to learn how to set it up, and our security whitepaper (opens in new tab) for how the architecture works, or deploy it through consulting partners like Accenture, Deloitte, KPMG, and PwC.

articles.title: Introducing Claude Ship
articles.context: For most customers, we recommend enabling this first in observe-only mode to build confidence before configuring branch protection to require Claude Approvals' green light
articles.full_text:
Anyone who has opened a pull request knows how this goes. They start on the next thing, and then the review comes back. So they stop, dig back into the old code, push a fix, and wait for the review to run again. Then they go find someone to approve it.

There's a good reason it works this way. Most teams want a person to approve every change, and that's easy to keep up with when people write every line. But a lot of developers build with agents now. On the Claude Code team, Claude writes most of our code, and we wanted everything after the PR to move that fast too.

That's why we built Claude Ship, available today in beta. It can review PRs, fix them, and decide what's ready to merge based on policies each team sets. Teams stay in control of where it runs and which changes need a person. The goal: ship code as fast as teams write it.

Eligible Claude Enterprise organizations can claim at least $10,000 in Claude Ship credits to use within 30 days of claiming. Claim by January 15, 2027. Terms apply.

How Claude Ship works: review, fix, and approve

Claude Ship is made up of Code Review, which is already generally available, and two new agents in beta: PR Steward and Claude Approvals. Together, they take a pull request through review, fixes, and an approval decision so teams don't have to manage each step manually.

Code Review performs an in-depth review of pull requests against the codebase through multiple lenses. It collects findings, adversarially verifies them, categorizes them, and posts them to a PR. On the Claude Code team, where Claude's review is one layer of a broader process, merged PRs more than doubled from June to September while the share reverted fell by more than 40%. Code Review gives teams fast reviews, clear findings, and a choice of Quick, Standard, or Deep review levels for each repository.

PR Steward works to keep a PR green, but is designed not to approve or merge pull requests. It jumps in on failing CI checks, merge conflicts, and review feedback from Code Review, other review tools, or team members. After every push, it comments with what it changed and how to undo it. Developers can comment @claude with an instruction to steer the work, or @claude stop to have it step back.

From there, Claude Approvals applies an approval policy that the team writes as a file in the repository. Claude can approve routine changes on its own if the policy allows it, or can require deeper human sign-off for certain scenarios. It works like a smarter CODEOWNERS file. Teams can have Claude Approvals consider a variety of signals in its decision-making process, including Code Review findings or their own classifiers using natural language. For most customers, we recommend enabling this first in observe-only mode to build confidence before configuring branch protection to require Claude Approvals' green light.

Two ways to get started

For developers: /ship it from Claude Code

Developers can try Claude Ship on their own pull requests with the new /ship command in Claude Code. When a change is ready, they run /ship. Claude pushes it, opens the PR, reviews the change, and works on feedback and failing checks to help get it ready to merge. What can merge depends on the developer's permissions and the repository's branch rules.

For admins and engineering leaders: set the rules, one repository at a time

Turning Claude Ship on for an entire repository puts it to work across a team's pull requests automatically, under settings and an approval policy the team controls. Developers don't need to manually invoke the /ship command.

Admins choose where it runs. An admin turns on Code Review and PR Steward for each repository. Claude Approvals starts when a connected repository has a policy file on its default branch, and an admin can turn it off.

Each repository gets the settings it needs. Admins choose the review level (Quick, Standard, or Deep), choose when reviews run, and configure spend limits.

Teams keep the tools they have. Claude Ship works with existing branch protection and required checks.

Teams set the pace. They can start with one repository, choose a review level and when reviews run, set a monthly spend limit, and run their approval policy in observe mode until they trust it.

How the Claude Code team ships

We run Claude Ship on many of our own pull requests. One of the biggest changes is who can act on customer feedback. For example, a product manager on the Claude Code team can now read a piece of feedback, talk through ideas and tradeoffs with Claude Tag, have it open a PR, and move on to the next thing while Claude Ship takes it through review, fixes, and an approval decision.

Recently, a customer was confused because our Analytics API documentation implied an Admin key could pull Pro and Team usage. The PM asked Claude Tag whether a fix was in flight, and it opened one. Code Review found nothing blocking, a docs reviewer signed off, Claude Approvals passed, and the fix merged that same evening.

Attackers don’t need to compromise every security control; they just need to exploit a gap. As users become more distributed, applications and data spread across hybrid environments, and unmanaged and agentless assets proliferate, security teams face an increasing number of visibility gaps that attackers can exploit.

At the same time, AI is enabling adversaries to operate at greater speed and scale, accelerating established attack techniques such as credential compromise and vulnerability exploitation.1 This shift is already visible: Verizon’s 2026 Data Breach Investigations Report found that exploitation of vulnerabilities has overtaken credential abuse and phishing as the leading initial-access vector for breaches.2

Against this backdrop, the network becomes a critical vantage point for defenders, providing visibility into activity and behavior across the environment. Preventive controls remain essential, but no single control sees the entire attack. Network Detection and Response (NDR) helps close these visibility gaps by analyzing network traffic for suspicious behavior, giving security teams additional context to investigate threats, including across unmanaged and agentless assets.

Gartner’s outlook for the category reflects NDR’s growing importance: “The NDR market will continue to grow over the next decade, evolving from a niche security product to a critical one. As user behaviors are increasingly obfuscated by encryption and attackers are increasingly hiding their activities in ‘living off the land’ techniques, NDR will be critical in identifying both insider threats and threats that are launched from internally compromised hosts.”3

To address thes challenges, the new Sophos NDR gives organizations broader visibility across the network, active prevention capabilities, flexible deployment options, and network intelligence connected through Sophos Fusion.

Comprehensive network detection and response for the AI era

Originally introduced as an add-on to Sophos Managed Detection and Response (MDR) or Extended Detection and Response (XDR) in 2024, Sophos NDR is now available as a standalone solution.

What’s new in Sophos NDR:

Converged protection

Behavioral detection and Intrusion Detection and Prevention Systems (IDS/IPS) in one solution for known and unknown threats.

Dedicated Sophos NDR hardware

New purpose-built Sophos hardware for NDR workloads.

Active inline response

On dedicated Sophos NDR hardware, inspect traffic in real time and automatically block identified malicious traffic.

Available standalone

Purchase Sophos NDR as a standalone solution.

Deployment flexibility

Virtual, compatible third-party hardware, or dedicated Sophos NDR hardware, with passive and active inspection options.

Connected through Sophos Fusion

Centralized management, shared context, and coordinated response across Sophos Fusion.

“Network visibility provides an important layer of defense, particularly for devices and activity that preventive controls alone may not see. Sophos NDR builds on that visibility by combining behavioral network detection with active prevention and connecting network intelligence with context from across the Sophos Fusion defense system. This approach gives security teams greater context to investigate suspicious activity and coordinate response across the broader security environment.”

– Chris Kissel, Research Vice President at IDC

See more across the network

Known threats and unfamiliar attack behavior require different approaches. Signature-based inspection helps identify known malicious activity, while behavioral analytics help uncover suspicious patterns that don’t match a known signature.

The new Sophos NDR brings these capabilities together:

AI- and ML-powered behavioral analytics help identify suspicious network activity and unknown threats.

Encrypted traffic analysis helps uncover malicious patterns in encrypted communications without requiring full decryption.

Network analytics and threat hunting give security teams additional context to investigate suspicious activity.

Deep packet inspection and IDS/IPS capabilities add signature-based detection and, in supported configurations, inline prevention of known threats.

Together, these capabilities help organizations identify lateral movement, command-and-control communications, and unexpected data movement—including activity involving unmanaged and agentless assets.

This network perspective helps teams investigate activity that may not be visible to endpoint or firewall protection alone.

Stop threats faster: putting the “R” in NDR

A detection can tell you something is wrong. Active Inline mode adds the ability to act directly in the traffic path.

On a dedicated Sophos NDR appliance with the optional IDS/IPS Add-on, Active Inline mode inspects live traffic and automatically blocks known malicious packets before they reach their destination.

For organizations that want monitoring without enforcement, Sophos NDR also offers passive deployment modes. Customers can choose the approach that fits their network architecture and operational requirements.

Deploy your way

Network environments aren’t all built the same. Sophos NDR gives customers a choice of virtual and physical deployment options:

Virtual appliances for supported virtualized and cloud environments.

New Sophos NDR hardware, purpose-built for NDR workloads.

Compatible third-party hardware for organizations that want to use their own supported infrastructure.

Three traffic inspection modes provide further flexibility, depending on the hardware and configuration:

SPAN/TAP: Analyze a mirrored copy of traffic without placing the sensor in the live traffic path.

Passive Inline: Inspect traffic in the network path without actively blocking it.

Active Inline: Inspect traffic in the network path and block known malicious packets.

Active Inline mode requires a dedicated Sophos NDR appliance with the IDS/IPS add-on. Virtual appliances and compatible third-party hardware do not provide active inline blocking.

Network context. Coordinated defense.

Network evidence becomes more valuable when teams can connect it to what’s happening elsewhere. Through Sophos Fusion, Sophos NDR connects network telemetry, detections, and context with insights from endpoint, firewall, identity, email, and cloud security. This shared context strengthens Sophos MDR and XDR investigations and coordinated response.

articles.title: Introducing the new AWS WAF security analytics dashboard
articles.context: You can also see which detections and labels matched and whether each action was enforced or only counted
articles.full_text:
When blocked requests spike or a customer reports being locked out, a security team has to work out what is happening, where it is happening, and if AWS WAF is making the right call. Currently, that usually means opening each protection pack (web ACL) in turn, across domains, AWS Regions, and Amazon CloudFront distributions, or querying AWS WAF logs. In 2024, we introduced the AWS WAF traffic overview dashboard, which gives you a near real-time view of each protection pack (web ACL). Today, we’re introducing the AWS WAF security analytics dashboard: a single global page that you can use to investigate traffic across all of your protection packs (web ACLs), Regional resources, Amazon CloudFront distributions and then act on what you find. The dashboard can help you investigate and contain threats faster and reduce false positives that block real customers. You don’t need to build or maintain your own log analytics pipeline to do it.

In this post, we introduce the new dashboard and walk you through two use cases: investigating a traffic spike, and tuning your rules to reduce false positives.

Introduction to the security analytics dashboard

To open the dashboard, go to the AWS WAF console and choose Security analytics in the navigation pane. The dashboard shows request data across all protection packs (web ACLs) in your account. You can narrow it to specific protection packs (web ACLs) and set the time range. As shown in the following figure, at the top of the page, you can see total requests split by action (Allow, Block, CAPTCHA, and Challenge). The Requests chart shows how the traffic changes over time. Below that, traffic breakdown widgets show the top values for each dimension. The dashboard is built on full-fidelity request data, not samples.

Figure 1: The security analytics dashboard across all protection packs

Dimensions

You can filter, group, and break down traffic by dimensions that include, but aren’t limited to, the following:

Who’s sending traffic – Client IP, country, Autonomous System Number (ASN), user-agent, and JA4 TLS fingerprints

What they’re requesting – Host, path (URI), protected resource (Amazon CloudFront distribution, AWS Application Load Balancers, and others), Region, or protection pack (web ACL)

How AWS WAF responded – Action, rule triggered, labels, or response code

We’ll continue to add dimensions to the security analytics dashboard over time. The rest of this post refers to the preceding dimensions by the names used here. Two dimensions deserve a closer look:

Host – Many customers think about their applications by domain rather than by protection pack (web ACL). Grouping or filtering by Host will show you which of your domains are under attack or if a spike is hitting www, the API, or a staging site, even when one protection pack (web ACL) protects several domains or one domain spans several protection packs (web ACLs).

Labels – Labels are metadata that AWS WAF rules add to the requests they inspect. AWS Managed Rules for AWS WAF add them (for example, Bot Control labels for bot category, verification status, and signals such as non_browser_user_agent), and you can create rules to add custom labels. Because labels are recorded even when a rule only counts, filtering by a label shows you what a rule detected across all of your protection packs (web ACLs), without changing how your traffic is handled.

Controls

The dashboard is built around a few controls:

Filter requests – Combine conditions on any dimension, using Equals or Does not equal. Filters apply to the whole dashboard: the action split, the Requests chart, every widget, and the request list update to match. Your dashboard view is saved in your browser.

Group by – Split the Requests chart by any dimension, such as Host, Rule triggered, Country, or JA4, to see how traffic changes over time.

Show only, Exclude, and Block – Select any value in any widget to focus on it, remove it from view, or block it. For example, you can block a high-risk or unexpected IP address, or block traffic from a country, directly from the dashboard.

Requests and detections – Review the individual requests behind the charts. For each request, see HTTP request fields such as host, path, headers, user agent, and JA4 fingerprint. You can also see which detections and labels matched and whether each action was enforced or only counted . Previously, this level of detail meant working from a limited sample of requests or setting up and querying your own AWS WAF logs. Now it’s available directly on the dashboard.

Together, these controls help you answer questions such as:

What share of traffic across all your protection packs (web ACLs) and domains is being blocked, challenged, or allowed, and how is it changing?

Which rules are doing the most work, and are any of them blocking legitimate users?

Which IP addresses, ASNs, JA4 fingerprints, or countries are behind a spike, and what are they targeting?

How much of your traffic comes from bots, and are the bots verified?

Use case 1: Investigate a traffic spike

Suppose you receive an alert that blocked requests have increased. To investigate:

Go to the Security analytics page in the AWS WAF console and select All protection packs.

Assess the scope: The action split shows the overall block rate. Group the Requests chart by Host to see which domains are affected and check the Protection pack widget to see whether one application or several are involved. A campaign hitting your storefront, API, and media domains at the same time calls for a different response than a problem on a single endpoint.

Identify the source: Group the Requests chart by Rule triggered to see which rules are mitigating the traffic and when they started firing. Then check the source and request dimensions. If one IP address sends a disproportionate share of requests, or many IP addresses share one JA4 fingerprint, the traffic likely originates from a single automated actor.

Figure 2: Requests grouped by Rule triggered, showing which rules fired and when

Confirm with request-level evidence: When you find an unexpected value, select it and choose Show only to filter the entire dashboard to it.

Then confirm what you’re seeing in Requests and detections. Expanding a request shows all its details, including the HTTP request fields. For example, a curl user agent with no Accept-Language header, coming from a cloud hosting ASN, is likely automated traffic.

Figure 3: Show only, exclude, or block it

After you confirm the source, choose a response that fits the traffic:

One clear source: Choose Block this IP address directly from the dashboard. Use a geographic block only if you don’t expect legitimate customers from that country.

Traffic spread across multiple IP addresses: Add a rate-based rule with a custom aggregation key such as JA4, or use AWS WAF Bot Control.

Known bad actors and application-layer floods: Add the Amazon IP reputation list and the Anti-DDoS managed rule group.

Faster detection time: Create Amazon CloudWatch alarms on AWS WAF metrics. For details, see Monitoring with Amazon CloudWatch.

When the change is in place, return to the dashboard to confirm that requests from that source now show the Block action.

Use case 2: Tune your rules and reduce false positives

Rules can fail in two ways: by blocking legitimate users, or by only counting traffic that they should stop. Filters and labels help you find both.

If you suspect that a rule is blocking a broad population, such as many distinct clients sending only a few requests each, enter Rule triggered = <rule name> in Filter requests. The dashboard shows only the requests that the rule acted on. Review the Country, Host, and Path (URI) breakdowns to understand who the blocked clients are and what they requested. If the blocked clients look like your typical customers, with common browsers, expected countries, and checkout or login paths, consider adding a scope-down statement to the rule or changing the action to Challenge.

Figure 4: The dashboard filtered to a single rule with Filter requests

Evaluate rules before you enforce them: When you evaluate a managed rule group in Count mode, filter by its labels to see exactly which requests each rule matched. For example, filter by a Bot Control label such as awswaf:managed:aws:bot-control:bot:unverified, then check Host, Path (URI), and User-Agent to see what those bots are after. Use Exclude on labels for known-good traffic, such as bot:verified search engine crawlers, to keep them out of your review.

On the Detections tab of Requests and detections, rows marked Counted, not enforced show what a rule would block. If the matches aren’t partners or monitoring tools, consider changing the rule action to Block.

Figure 5: Record details for a single request, including host, JA4 fingerprint, and protection pack

After you change a rule, compare the same time window on the dashboard to confirm that the rule now affects only the traffic you intended.

Conclusion

The traffic overview dashboard shows you what changed in each protection pack (web ACL). The security analytics dashboard helps you understand why it changed, and lets you act on it from the same page, across all of your protection packs (web ACLs), domains, Regions, and Amazon CloudFront distributions. Filters, grouping, and labels explain the traffic, and request-level evidence helps you act with more confidence. Together, they can help you investigate faster, reduce how often real users are blocked by mistake, and confirm that each rule changes affect the traffic you intend.

The security analytics dashboard is available at no extra cost in all AWS Regions where AWS WAF is offered, and shows up to 21 days of request data. To get started, open the AWS WAF console and choose Security analytics.

If you have feedback about this post, submit comments in the Comments section below.

articles.title: Identity context is essential for exposure management: Tenable One adds ways to bring in identity security data
articles.context: Attackers often chain identity flaws with other security issues, such as vulnerabilities and misconfigurations, to create attack paths to your most critical systems and data
articles.full_text:
Tenable One now ingests identity findings from third-party sources, allowing you to assess and prioritize exposures related to stale and overprivileged accounts alongside your other security data, such as vulnerabilities and misconfigurations.

Key takeaways

Managing identity risk should be an essential part of any exposure management program. However, in many organizations, exposure management programs often don’t include their identity-security teams.

Relying on siloed identity-security teams and tools leaves organizations vulnerable to attackers who chain identity flaws with other infrastructure vulnerabilities.

Tenable One now ingests findings from third-party identity security providers, so that you can prioritize such findings alongside all other types of exposures in your attack surface.

If your exposure management program can’t see identity risk, it’s missing a key piece of puzzle. According to SANS Institute’s “2026 State of Identity Threats & Defenses Survey Insights Event” report, 55% of organizations suffered at least one identity-related breach during the 12-month survey period, and among those organizations, 21% suffered more than one breach.

Attackers often chain identity flaws with other security issues, such as vulnerabilities and misconfigurations, to create attack paths to your most critical systems and data. However, in many security programs, identity security is siloed and managed by a separate team with its own tools.

This is a significant problem. Identity risk simply can’t be managed in isolation. It belongs in your exposure management program, so that you can address identity exposures alongside other exposures in your on-premises infrastructure, cloud workloads, IoT devices, operational technology (OT) systems, and AI tools.

Many organizations have already invested in identity security tools they trust, and they shouldn’t have to replace those tools in order to manage identity findings in the Tenable One Exposure Management Platform. The Tenable One Identity Exposure domain in Tenable One is designed to solve this problem by bringing in relevant data from third-party identity tools.

Two new ways to bring identity security data into Tenable One

Tenable One now supports two new methods to ingest third-party identity data: first, a dedicated connector for Semperis Lightning; and second, custom ingestion of identity findings through the Tenable One Open Connector. Alongside Tenable One Identity Exposure, customers now have more choices in how they discover and manage identity risk within their exposure management program.

These two new ways to bring identity security data into Tenable One give your security team one picture of your organization’s cyber risk. Identity misconfigurations, stale accounts, and excessive privilege come into Tenable One as exposures to prioritize alongside your other security issues such as vulnerabilities and cloud misconfigurations, as part of the Tenable One dashboards and reports your team already uses.

Having identity security findings in one place reduces the chance that they’ll get overlooked. Stale and overprivileged accounts pile up quietly, and cleaning them up has usually meant logging in to your identity tool, exporting a list, and reviewing it. Now your team can weigh them against all your other security issues when deciding what to fix next, and focus on the riskiest accounts before an attacker finds them.

Bring Active Directory and Entra ID data from Semperis using the Tenable connector

Our first dedicated identity connector is for Semperis Lightning, which is designed to continuously monitor Active Directory and Microsoft Entra ID for identity misconfigurations, privilege abuse, stale accounts, and authentication weaknesses. The connector brings accounts, groups and roles as assets in Tenable One.

Take a stale service account with a tier 0 privilege, the most privileged tier in Microsoft’s enterprise access model. Semperis flags it as an indicator of exposure (IoE), with a severity rating, a description, and remediation guidance. The connector brings that IoE into Tenable One as a finding on the account itself, with its severity rating and the steps to remediate. Tenable One logs the account’s privileged designation as a tag, so your team can see it at a glance.

The connector also keeps Tenable One and Semperis Lightning automatically in sync. When your team fixes the problem and the IoE passes its next Semperis check, the finding moves to the Fixed queue in Tenable One.

You also control what identity security data gets imported into Tenable One. You can choose to ingest data from Active Directory, Entra ID, or both, and you can filter out findings by picking a minimum severity level.

How to Bring Semperis Identity Data into Tenable One, Identify Crown Jewel Accounts, and Act on Findings. The demo covers connecting Semperis to Tenable One, locating key assets, and moving from findings to remediation. Connecting the data source: In Connectors, add a new connector and filter by the Identity Security category. Configure the Semperis connector to ingest identity security data directly into Tenable One. For other identity providers, the Tenable One Open Connector is designed to bring security data from custom sources into the platform, including another identity security tool, a homegrown system, or a spreadsheet. Analyzing assets: In Assets, filter the view by Semperis to isolate identity security data. The view shows 11.3k assets imported from Semperis, including 44 new assets in the last 7 days. Accounts are the asset type attackers typically target first, so open the Accounts asset type and add a filter for crown jewel accounts. The resulting list of crown jewel account assets is sorted by number of active findings. Investigating findings: Open an account with 14 active findings, including several critical findings. The account page shows full details, including account type and relevant tags. The findings list for the account is ranked by severity. Open an individual finding to see the details needed to understand the issue and decide how to fix it. Remediation: Use Tenable Hexa AI for remediation. With a simple prompt it can create separate JIRA tickets for each critical finding, including all relevant details. Complete the action and send the ticket to move from finding to fix and close the gap.

Ingest identity data from other sources with the Tenable One Open Connector

Tenable One Open Connector brings security data from custom sources into the platform, and now it accepts identity data too, whether it lives in another identity security tool, a homegrown system, or a spreadsheet.

Open Connector also handles the mechanics. Connect to your cloud or storage database of choice and Tenable One picks up new files automatically as they refresh. Prefer to do it by hand? Upload CSV, Excel, or ZIP files directly. You decide how your identity security tools fields map to Tenable One’s, including combining them or keeping them separate. Tenable One then deduplicates and normalizes the data, so an account reported by two sources shows up as one finding.

Also new: More connectors for application security, and asset inventory tools

Identity is the newest category we have added to Tenable One Open Connector, which currently features more than 400 validated integrations. However, it’s not the only area in which we’re adding connectors. We’ve shipped nine new Tenable One Connectors for application security and endpoint tools.

Application security: GitHub Code Scanning, GitHub Dependabot, GitLab, Veracode SAST, Veracode SCA, Invicti, and Checkmarx

Asset inventory: ChromeOS, Asimily

Learn how to set up the Semperis connector and check out all available Tenable One connectors.
